SECTION 1 — THE ANSWERS
=====================================================================

1.1 SERVICE CONTRACT — the withdrawal period expires at the end of 14 days from the day of the conclusion of the contract. Source: Article 9(2)(a) of [PS1] ("in the case of service contracts, the day of the conclusion of the contract"), read with Article 9(1) of [PS1].

1.2 SALES CONTRACT — the withdrawal period expires at the end of 14 days from the day on which the consumer, or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by the consumer, acquires physical possession of the goods. Source: Article 9(2)(b) of [PS1], read with Article 9(1) of [PS1].

1.3 Both answers are subject to Article 10 of [PS1] (omission of the information on the right of withdrawal), which extends the period to 12 months and can restart it for a further 14 days — Section 5 below. Both are also subject to the 30-day option in Article 9(1a) of [PS1], inserted by [PS2], where the applicable national law has taken that option up — paragraph 3.2 below.

=====================================================================
SECTION 2 — THE GOVERNING TEXT
=====================================================================

2.1 Article 9(1) of [PS1]: "The consumer shall have a period of 14 days to withdraw from a distance or off-premises contract, without giving any reason, and without incurring any costs other than those provided for in Article 13(2) and Article 14."

2.2 Article 9(2) of [PS1] (as consolidated): "Without prejudice to Article 10, the withdrawal period referred to in paragraph 1 of this Article shall expire after 14 days or, in cases where Member States have adopted rules in accordance with paragraph 1a of this Article, 30 days from:
(a) in the case of service contracts, the day of the conclusion of the contract;
(b) in the case of sales contracts, the day on which the consumer or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by the consumer acquires physical possession of the goods or:
(i) in the case of multiple goods ordered by the consumer in one order and delivered separately, the day on which the consumer or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by the consumer acquires physical possession of the last good;
(ii) in the case of delivery of a good consisting of multiple lots or pieces, the day on which the consumer or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by the consumer acquires physical possession of the last lot or piece;
(iii) in the case of contracts for regular delivery of goods during defined period of time, the day on which the consumer or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by the consumer acquires physical possession of the first good;
(c) in the case of contracts for the supply of water, gas or electricity, where they are not put up for sale in a limited volume or set quantity, of district heating or of digital content which is not supplied on a tangible medium, the day of the conclusion of the contract."

2.3 Article 10 of [PS1] (as consolidated): "Omission of information on the right of withdrawal
1. If the trader has not provided the consumer with the information on the right of withdrawal as required by point (h) of Article 6(1), the withdrawal period shall expire 12 months from the end of the initial withdrawal period, as determined in accordance with Article 9(2).
2. If the trader has provided the consumer with the information provided for in paragraph 1 of this Article within 12 months from the day referred to in Article 9(2), the withdrawal period shall expire 14 days or, in cases where Member States have adopted rules in accordance with Article 9(1a), 30 days after the day upon which the consumer receives that information."

2.4 Article 6(1) of [PS1], chapeau: the information listed in points (a) to (t) must be given "Before the consumer is bound by a distance or off-premises contract, or any corresponding offer ... in a clear and comprehensible manner". Point (h) is "where a right of withdrawal exists, the conditions, time limit and procedures for exercising that right in accordance with Article 9(1), as well as the model withdrawal form set out in Annex I(B)".

2.5 Article 6(4) of [PS1]: "The information referred to in points (h), (i) and (j) of paragraph 1 of this Article may be provided by means of the model instructions on withdrawal set out in Annex I(A). The trader shall have fulfilled the information requirements laid down in points (h), (i) and (j) of paragraph 1 of this Article if the trader has supplied these instructions to the consumer, correctly filled in. The references to the withdrawal period of 14 days in the model instructions on withdrawal set out in Annex I(A) shall be replaced by references to a withdrawal period of 30 days in cases where Member States have adopted rules in accordance with Article 9(1a)."

2.6 Article 6(6) of [PS1]: "If the trader has not complied with the information requirements on additional charges or other costs as referred to in point (e) of paragraph 1, or on the costs of returning the goods as referred to in point (i) of paragraph 1, the consumer shall not bear those charges or costs."

2.7 Article 6(9) of [PS1]: the burden of proof in respect of compliance with the information requirements laid down in Chapter III is on the trader.

2.8 Article 7(3) of [PS1]: "Where a consumer wants the performance of services, or the supply of water, gas or electricity, where they are not put up for sale in a limited volume or set quantity, or of district heating to begin during the withdrawal period provided for in Article 9(2), and the contract places the consumer under an obligation to pay, the trader shall require that the consumer make such an express request on a durable medium and request the consumer to acknowledge that, once the contract has been fully performed by the trader, the consumer will no longer have the right of withdrawal."

2.9 Article 16(a) of [PS1]: Member States shall not provide for the right of withdrawal set out in Articles 9 to 15 in respect of distance and off-premises contracts as regards "service contracts after the service has been fully performed if the performance has begun with the consumer's prior express consent, and with the acknowledgement that he will lose his right of withdrawal once the contract has been fully performed by the trader". The list in Article 16 is closed for distance and off-premises contracts.

2.10 Article 14(3) of [PS1]: where the consumer exercises the right of withdrawal after having made a request in accordance with Article 7(3) or Article 8(8), the consumer pays an amount proportionate to what has been provided until the consumer informed the trader of the withdrawal, in comparison with the full coverage of the contract.

2.11 Article 13(1) of [PS1]: the trader reimburses all payments received from the consumer, including, where applicable, the costs of delivery, without undue delay and in any event not later than 14 days from the day on which the trader is informed of the consumer's decision to withdraw.

2.12 Article 2 of [PS1], definitions: "'sales contract' means any contract under which the trader transfers or undertakes to transfer the ownership of goods to the consumer and the consumer pays or undertakes to pay the price thereof, including any contract having as its object both goods and services"; "'service contract' means any contract other than a sales contract under which the trader supplies or undertakes to supply a service to the consumer and the consumer pays or undertakes to pay the price thereof".

=====================================================================
SECTION 3 — SERVICE CONTRACTS: RULE, FORMULA, EARLY EXTINCTION
=====================================================================

3.1 Trigger. The period runs from the day of the conclusion of the contract (Article 9(2)(a) of [PS1]). It does not run from the day performance begins, from the day the consumer pays, or from the day the consumer first uses the service. For an online retailer, the date of conclusion is determined by the applicable national law of contract formation (offer/acceptance, order confirmation), which is a national-law question outside the Directive and must be fixed in the retailer's terms so that the date is objectively ascertainable.

3.2 Length. 14 days (Article 9(1) and 9(2) of [PS1]). 30 days applies only if the Member State has adopted rules under Article 9(1a) of [PS1] (inserted by [PS2]); where it has, every reference to 14 days in Articles 9 and 10 and in Annex I(A) is replaced by 30 days (Article 6(4) third sentence and Article 10(2) of [PS1]). Do not use 30 days unless the applicable national law has taken up that option.

3.3 Formula. Expiry = C + N, where C = the date of conclusion of the contract and N = 14 days (30 days only under Article 9(1a)). The period expires at the end of the last day. Day-counting convention: Section 6.

3.4 The period can be cut short, and the right lost, before the 14 days run out. Under Article 16(a) of [PS1], the right of withdrawal does not exist for a service contract once the service has been fully performed, provided (i) performance began with the consumer's prior express consent and (ii) the consumer acknowledged that the right is lost on full performance. Article 7(3) of [PS1] prescribes how the trader must obtain those two elements for a distance contract: the consumer must make an express request on a durable medium to begin performance during the withdrawal period, and the trader must request the acknowledgement. Consequences for drafting:
  (a) A request for early performance, standing alone, does not extinguish the right. A request plus performance begun but not completed does not extinguish the right either: Article 16(a) requires full performance. The right survives until the service is fully performed or the 14 days expire, whichever is first.
  (b) If the trader has not obtained the express request on a durable medium and the acknowledgement, Article 16(a) does not apply, the right survives the full 14 days, and Article 14(3) does not apply either — so no proportionate payment is owed for the pre-withdrawal period.
  (c) For continuing services (e.g. a 12-month subscription), full performance is not reached during the withdrawal period, so the right is never extinguished early by Article 16(a); the consumer who withdraws after performance has begun owes the proportionate amount under Article 14(3), and the Annex I(A) sentence in paragraph 7.1(c) below must be included.
  (d) Illustration: contract concluded 1 March 2025; consumer expressly requests on a durable medium on 3 March that performance begin and acknowledges loss of the right; service fully performed on 10 March. The right of withdrawal is extinguished on 10 March 2025, five days before the 14-day period would otherwise have expired. If instead the service is only partly performed by 12 March and the consumer withdraws on 12 March, the right subsists and Article 14(3) applies.

3.5 Worked example (service contract concluded 1 March 2025, 14-day baseline):
  - Convention A (trigger day not counted): days 1–14 are 2 to 15 March 2025; the period expires at the end of 15 March 2025.
  - Convention B (trigger day counted): days 1–14 are 1 to 14 March 2025; the period expires at the end of 14 March 2025.
  (Conventions defined in Section 6.)

=====================================================================
SECTION 4 — SALES CONTRACTS: RULE, FORMULA, SUB-CASES, NON-DELIVERY
=====================================================================

4.1 Trigger. Physical possession. The period runs from the day on which the consumer, or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by the consumer, acquires physical possession of the goods (Article 9(2)(b) of [PS1]). Two points follow from the words used:
  (a) Handing the goods to the carrier is not the trigger. Delivery to a locker, to a pick-up point, or to a neighbour counts only if the neighbour is a third party indicated by the consumer — the carrier and its agents are expressly excluded.
  (b) Where the consumer indicates a third party (e.g. a gift recipient), that third party's possession starts the period.

4.2 Sub-cases under Article 9(2)(b)(i)–(iii) of [PS1]:
  (i) multiple goods ordered in one order and delivered separately — the day the consumer acquires physical possession of the LAST good;
  (ii) a good consisting of multiple lots or pieces — the day the consumer acquires physical possession of the LAST lot or piece;
  (iii) contracts for regular delivery of goods during a defined period — the day the consumer acquires physical possession of the FIRST good.

4.3 Goods supplied as water, gas or electricity (not put up for sale in a limited volume or set quantity), district heating, or digital content not supplied on a tangible medium: the trigger is the day of the conclusion of the contract (Article 9(2)(c) of [PS1]). Where the retailer sells digital content not on a tangible medium, the trigger is therefore the conclusion date, not a download date, and Article 16(m) of [PS1] governs the separate question of when the right is lost for such content.

4.4 Mixed contracts. A contract with both goods and services as its object is a sales contract under the Article 2 definition in [PS1] ("including any contract having as its object both goods and services"). The delivery trigger in Article 9(2)(b) therefore applies to a bundle of, say, a device plus an installation or a subscription. Where the service element is to begin within the withdrawal period, Article 7(3) of [PS1] still applies to that element.

4.5 Non-delivery — correction of a premise in the instructions. There is no rule that a trader's failure to deliver within the withdrawal period extends the period to 12 months. Article 10 of [PS1] has only two paragraphs (the consolidated text moves directly from Article 10(2) to the heading of Article 11), and [PS2] amended Article 10(2) only. On the Directive's text, if physical possession is never acquired, the Article 9(2)(b) trigger never occurs and the 14-day withdrawal period never begins to run; the consumer's remedy for non-delivery lies in [PS3] and the applicable national law, not in an extension of the withdrawal period. A national implementing measure could in principle add a fallback trigger, which is a point to check — but it cannot be assumed.

4.6 Worked examples (14-day baseline):
  - Single good, possession acquired 1 March 2025: Convention A → expiry end of 15 March 2025; Convention B → expiry end of 14 March 2025.
  - Multiple goods in one order delivered separately, last good possessed 20 April 2025: Convention A → 21–30 April (10 days) + 1–4 May (4 days) = 14; expiry end of 4 May 2025. Convention B → 20–30 April (11 days) + 1–3 May (3 days) = 14; expiry end of 3 May 2025.
  - Regular delivery during a defined period, first good possessed 1 March 2025: expiry as for the single good above, regardless of how many later deliveries follow.

=====================================================================
SECTION 5 — THE ARTICLE 10 EXTENSION (BOTH CONTRACT TYPES)
=====================================================================

5.1 Initial period omitted information — Article 10(1) of [PS1]. If the trader has not provided the information required by Article 6(1)(h), the period expires 12 months from the END of the initial withdrawal period determined under Article 9(2). Note the anchor: it is the end of the initial period, not the trigger day.

5.2 Late provision within the window — Article 10(2) of [PS1]. If the trader provides that information within 12 months from the DAY referred to in Article 9(2) (i.e. from the trigger day), the period expires 14 days (30 days where Article 9(1a) has been adopted) after the day the consumer receives the information. Note the different anchor from Article 10(1).

5.3 Outer bound. The two paragraphs meet at the same instant: under Article 10(1) the period cannot run beyond trigger day + 14 days + 12 months; under Article 10(2) the latest possible restart is at trigger day + 12 months, giving expiry at trigger day + 12 months + 14 days. Information supplied after the 12-month window does not restart anything, because the period will already have expired under Article 10(1).

5.4 Worked example (service contract concluded 1 March 2025, no Article 6(1)(h) information supplied with the contract):
  - Convention A: initial period ends 15 March 2025; extended expiry end of 15 March 2026 (the outer bound).
  - Convention B: initial period ends 14 March 2025; extended expiry end of 14 March 2026.
  - If the information is received by the consumer on 10 June 2025 (within 12 months of 1 March 2025), the period expires 14 days after receipt: Convention A → 24 June 2025; Convention B → 23 June 2025.
  - If the information is received on 20 March 2026 (after the window), nothing restarts; the period expired on 15 March 2026 (Convention A).

5.5 Burden of proof. Under Article 6(9) of [PS1] the burden of proving that the Article 6(1)(h) information was supplied is on the trader. The retailer must therefore retain evidence of what was shown to the consumer, and when, at the pre-contractual stage.

5.6 Timing of the information. Article 6(1) of [PS1] requires the information to be given before the consumer is bound. Supplying the Annex I(A) instructions only in the post-contractual confirmation on a durable medium (Article 8(7) of [PS1]) is, on the conservative reading, not compliance with Article 6(1)(h), and would expose the retailer to the Article 10(1) extension. The instructions should be given before the order is placed and repeated in the confirmation.

5.7 Safe harbour. Under Article 6(4) of [PS1], supplying the Annex I(A) model instructions correctly filled in discharges the Article 6(1)(h), (i) and (j) duties. The wording in Section 7 is taken from Annex I(A) and should be used verbatim, with only the bracketed fields completed.

=====================================================================
SECTION 6 — COUNTING THE DAYS AND THE LAST DAY (FLAGGED, NOT RESOLVED)
=====================================================================

6.1 The Directive fixes the number of days and the trigger event. It does not lay down a method of counting: whether the trigger day itself counts, and how a last day falling on a Saturday, Sunday or public holiday is treated, are matters for the national law implementing [PS1]. [PS4] does not supply the answer, because it governs periods laid down in acts of the Union institutions, not periods fixed by a private contract under a directive.

6.2 Two conventions are in use, and the retailer's instructions must be consistent with whichever the governing national law adopts:
  - Convention A (trigger day not counted): day 1 is the day after the trigger; the period expires at the end of the 14th day after the trigger.
  - Convention B (trigger day counted): day 1 is the trigger day; the period expires at the end of the 14th day counting the trigger day.
  Every worked example in Sections 3, 4 and 5 is given under both conventions so that no figure in this draft depends on the point being resolved. The reviewing attorney should fix one convention per target market and strike the other.

6.3 The last day. Whether the period is extended where the last day is a non-working day, and whether public holidays in the consumer's Member State count, are national-law points. Flagged for confirmation.

6.4 Exercise before expiry. Article 11(1) of [PS1] requires the consumer to inform the trader of the decision to withdraw before the expiry of the period, using the Annex I(B) model form or any other unequivocal statement. The Annex I(A) instructions state that it is sufficient to send the communication before the period expires; that sentence must be retained verbatim.

=====================================================================
SECTION 7 — DRAFT WITHDRAWAL INSTRUCTIONS FOR INSERTION INTO THE RETAILER'S TERMS
=====================================================================

(Annex I(A) wording of [PS1], completed. Use the version that matches the contract; delete the alternatives. Where the applicable national law has adopted Article 9(1a) of [PS1], replace every "14 days" below with "30 days".)

7.1 SERVICE CONTRACT (and digital content not supplied on a tangible medium, and water/gas/electricity/district heating under Article 9(2)(c))

"Right of withdrawal
You have the right to withdraw from this contract within 14 days without giving any reason.
The withdrawal period will expire after 14 days from the day of the conclusion of the contract.
To exercise the right of withdrawal, you must inform us [trader's name, geographical address, telephone number and e-mail address] of your decision to withdraw from this contract by an unequivocal statement (e.g. a letter sent by post or e-mail). You may use the attached model withdrawal form, but it is not obligatory. You can also electronically fill in and submit the model withdrawal form or any other unequivocal statement on our website [internet address]. If you use this option, we will communicate to you an acknowledgement of receipt of such a withdrawal on a durable medium (e.g. by e-mail) without delay.
To meet the withdrawal deadline, it is sufficient for you to send your communication concerning your exercise of the right of withdrawal before the withdrawal period has expired.

Effects of withdrawal
If you withdraw from this contract, we shall reimburse to you all payments received from you, without undue delay and in any event not later than 14 days from the day on which we are informed about your decision to withdraw from this contract. We will carry out such reimbursement using the same means of payment as you used for the initial transaction, unless you have expressly agreed otherwise; in any event, you will not incur any fees as a result of such reimbursement.
If you requested to begin the performance of services during the withdrawal period, you shall pay us an amount which is in proportion to what has been provided until you have communicated us your withdrawal from this contract, in comparison with the full coverage of the contract."

Drafting notes to 7.1:
  (a) The final sentence tracks Article 14(3) of [PS1] and must appear wherever the retailer accepts an Article 7(3) express request for early performance. If the retailer does not accept early performance, delete the sentence and do not solicit the request.
  (b) The paragraph on the Article 16(a) loss of the right does not belong in the Annex I(A) block; if early performance is offered, put the Article 7(3) request and acknowledgement in a separate, separately-ticked checkout step, on a durable medium, and confirm it to the consumer under Article 8(7) of [PS1].
  (c) The "14 days" in the reimbursement paragraph is the Article 13(1) period and is a different period from the withdrawal period; do not change one without the other.

7.2 SALES CONTRACT — single good

"Right of withdrawal
You have the right to withdraw from this contract within 14 days without giving any reason.
The withdrawal period will expire after 14 days from the day on which you acquire, or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by you acquires, physical possession of the goods.
To exercise the right of withdrawal, you must inform us [trader's name, geographical address, telephone number and e-mail address] of your decision to withdraw from this contract by an unequivocal statement (e.g. a letter sent by post or e-mail). You may use the attached model withdrawal form, but it is not obligatory. You can also electronically fill in and submit the model withdrawal form or any other unequivocal statement on our website [internet address]. If you use this option, we will communicate to you an acknowledgement of receipt of such a withdrawal on a durable medium (e.g. by e-mail) without delay.
To meet the withdrawal deadline, it is sufficient for you to send your communication concerning your exercise of the right of withdrawal before the withdrawal period has expired.

Effects of withdrawal
If you withdraw from this contract, we shall reimburse to you all payments received from you, including the costs of delivery (with the exception of the supplementary costs resulting from your choice of a type of delivery other than the least expensive type of standard delivery offered by us), without undue delay and in any event not later than 14 days from the day on which we are informed about your decision to withdraw from this contract. We will carry out such reimbursement using the same means of payment as you used for the initial transaction, unless you have expressly agreed otherwise; in any event, you will not incur any fees as a result of such reimbursement.
We may withhold reimbursement until we have received the goods back or you have supplied evidence of having sent back the goods, whichever is the earliest.
You will have to bear the direct cost of returning the goods. [Alternative where the retailer bears them: We will bear the direct cost of returning the goods.]
You are only liable for any diminished value of the goods resulting from the handling other than what is necessary to establish the nature, characteristics and functioning of the goods."

7.3 SALES CONTRACT — the three sub-cases. Replace the second sentence of 7.2 with the following, as applicable:
  - multiple goods ordered in one order and delivered separately: "The withdrawal period will expire after 14 days from the day on which you acquire, or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by you acquires, physical possession of the last good."
  - a good consisting of multiple lots or pieces: "... physical possession of the last lot or piece."
  - regular delivery of goods during a defined period of time: "... physical possession of the first good."

7.4 MIXED GOODS-AND-SERVICES CONTRACT. Use 7.2 or 7.3 for the goods element (the contract is a sales contract under Article 2 of [PS1]) and add the Article 14(3) sentence from 7.1 only if early performance of the service element is offered and requested under Article 7(3).

7.5 MODEL WITHDRAWAL FORM (Annex I(B) of [PS1]) — to be attached to the instructions:

"Model withdrawal form
(complete and return this form only if you wish to withdraw from the contract)
— To [trader's name, geographical address and e-mail address]:
— I/We (*) hereby give notice that I/We (*) withdraw from my/our (*) contract of sale of the following goods (*)/for the provision of the following service (*),
— Ordered on (*)/received on (*),
— Name of consumer(s),
— Address of consumer(s),
— Signature of consumer(s) (only if this form is notified on paper),
— Date
(*) Delete as appropriate."

Note: Article 11(1) of [PS1] prohibits Member States from imposing formal requirements on the model form beyond those in Annex I(B). Do not add fields.

=====================================================================
SECTION 8 — CONFIRM BEFORE PUBLICATION (REVIEWING ATTORNEY)
=====================================================================

1. Identify the Member State(s) of the consumers targeted and obtain the implementing measure (for example, and to be verified rather than assumed: in Ireland, the European Union (Consumer Information, Cancellation and Other Rights) Regulations 2013; in Germany, §§ 312g, 355 and 356 BGB; in France, the Code de la consommation). Confirm the implementing text of Article 9(2), Article 10 and Annex I(A).
2. Confirm whether the Member State has adopted rules under Article 9(1a) of [PS1] (30-day period). If so, replace every "14 days" in Section 7 and every "N = 14" in Sections 3 to 5.
3. Fix the day-counting convention (Section 6.2) and the treatment of the last day falling on a non-working day or public holiday (Section 6.3) for each target market.
4. Confirm the contract-formation rule that fixes the "day of the conclusion of the contract" for the service contract, and make the checkout record the date unambiguously.
5. Confirm the delivery and possession evidence trail for the sales contract, including the identity of any third party indicated by the consumer and the treatment of split deliveries and partial shipments.
6. Confirm the Article 7(3) request-and-acknowledgement flow, its durable-medium record, and the Article 8(7) confirmation.
7. Confirm that the Annex I(A) and Annex I(B) text in Section 7 is verbatim against the consolidated text of [PS1] as amended by [PS2] at the date of publication.
8. Confirm that the pre-contractual information is delivered before the consumer is bound (Article 6(1) of [PS1]), not only in the post-contractual confirmation.
9. Confirm the record-keeping that discharges the Article 6(9) burden of proof.
10. Confirm whether any Member State has added a fallback trigger for goods never delivered (Section 4.5).

=====================================================================
SECTION 9 — CORRECTIONS TO THE INSTRUCTIONS GIVEN WITH THIS MATTER
=====================================================================

9.1 "Article 10(3) extends the period to 12 months where the trader fails to deliver within the withdrawal period" — there is no Article 10(3). Article 10 of [PS1] has two paragraphs. The extension in Article 10(1) is triggered only by omission of the Article 6(1)(h) information. Non-delivery is governed by [PS3] and national law (Section 4.5).

9.2 "A request under Article 7(3) ends the right on performance" — a request alone does not. The right is lost only on full performance, with prior express consent and acknowledgement (Article 16(a) of [PS1]); partial performance leaves the right intact and triggers proportionate payment under Article 14(3).

9.3 "12 months from the trigger day" as a description of Article 10(1) — the 12 months run from the END of the initial withdrawal period. Only the Article 10(2) window runs from the trigger day.

9.4 The brief does not mention Article 9(1a) (30 days). It must be checked for every target market.

9.5 The brief treats the periods as uniform across Member States. The Directive is a floor in places and leaves day-counting and non-working-day treatment to national law. The draft above therefore states the baseline and flags the national points rather than resolving them.

quotes.text: The presumption of innocence precludes a finding of guilt for a particular offence outside the criminal proceedings before the competent trial court, irrespective of the procedural safeguards in the parallel proceedings and notwithstanding general considerations of expediency. Thus, considering in one set of proceedings concerning a particular offence that an applicant has committed another offence which is subject to a trial in a parallel set of proceedings, is contrary to the applicant’s right to be presumed innocent with respect to that other offence (Kangers v. Latvia, 2019, §§ 60-61).

verdict.summary:
# ECHR Article 6 § 2 — The Presumption of Innocence: Verbatim Text, Full Citation and Verification Note

**Status:** Draft training material for review by a qualified attorney. Not legal advice. Every proposition of law below is tied to a primary source named in full; propositions drawn from secondary ECHR publications are labelled as such.

**Jurisdiction:** Council of Europe member States that are High Contracting Parties to the European Convention on Human Rights, as applied and interpreted by the European Court of Human Rights. Nothing here asserts that the presumption of innocence in this form binds courts outside that system; domestic-law equivalents must be checked separately in each jurisdiction.

---

## 1. The answer — verbatim text

**Article 6 § 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights, in the text presented as amended through Protocol No. 15:**

> “2. Everyone charged with a criminal offence shall be presumed innocent until proved guilty according to law.”

For a slide box without the paragraph number:

> “Everyone charged with a criminal offence shall be presumed innocent until proved guilty according to law.”

**Word-level accuracy points for the slide designer.** The sentence contains no internal punctuation and no semicolon; it ends with a single full stop. The operative words are “**proved**” (not “proven”), “**presumed innocent**” (not “presumed to be innocent”), and “**according to law**” (not “in accordance with law”, not “by law”). Variants of all three appear routinely in secondary summaries; any of them appearing in the module is a misquotation and should be corrected against the source at § 3 below.

**Answer to the “what presumption” question, stated plainly:** the presumption of innocence — Article 6 § 2 ECHR. It is a presumption operating in favour of “everyone charged with a criminal offence”, and it runs “until proved guilty according to law”.

---

## 2. Citation in full (use this form in the module's source note)

- **Convention:** Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (European Convention on Human Rights), Rome, 4 November 1950, **ETS No. 5**, Article 6 § 2, as amended by Protocol No. 11 (ETS No. 155), Protocol No. 14 (CETS No. 194) and Protocol No. 15 (CETS No. 213), consolidated English text published by the Council of Europe / European Court of Human Rights under the title *“European Convention on Human Rights, as amended by Protocols Nos. 11, 14 and 15, supplemented by Protocols Nos. 1, 4, 6, 7, 12, 13 and 16”*.
- **Amending instrument relied on for the “as amended through Protocol No. 15” constraint:** Protocol No. 15 amending the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, **CETS No. 213**, entered into force **1 August 2021**.
- **Court publication used for the interpretive gloss in § 6:** European Court of Human Rights, *Guide on Article 6 of the Convention – Right to a fair trial (criminal limb)*, last update 28 February 2026, § 362 and the Article 6 quotation box (secondary source; it reproduces the Article 6 text and cites the case law).

---

## 3. Verification that the quoted text is the Protocol No. 15 version

The constraint is that the text be the one “presented as amended through Protocol No. 15”. That is verified from the document's own front matter, quoted verbatim:

> “The text of the Convention is presented as amended by the provisions of Protocol No. 15 (CETS No. 213) as from its entry into force on 1 August 2021 and of Protocol No. 14 (CETS No. 194) as from its entry into force on 1 June 2010.”

Three further checks, each of which the reviewing attorney can repeat in under a minute:

1. **The cover title itself carries the constraint.** The consolidated English text is titled “as amended by Protocols Nos. 11, 14 and 15”.
2. **Amendments are footnoted where they occur, and Article 6 has no such footnote.** In the same consolidated text, provisions touched by Protocol No. 15 carry an express footnote — for example, the preamble sentence on subsidiarity and the margin of appreciation ends with footnote “1”, which reads: *“Text amended in accordance with the provisions of Protocol No. 15 (CETS No. 213) as from its entry into force on 1 August 2021.”* Article 6 § 2 carries no equivalent footnote in either consolidated version consulted. The absence is therefore meaningful, not an omission.
3. **Do not misread the page numbers.** In the ECHR PDF the digits “10 11” appear between Article 6 § 2 and § 3. Those are the printed page numbers of the booklet, not footnote markers and not amendment notes. Flagging this because it is an easy and embarrassing error to propagate into a slide.

**Limit of this verification, stated honestly:** the negative proposition “Protocol No. 15 did not amend Article 6 § 2” is supported here by the consolidated text's own footnote convention plus the absence of any footnote at Article 6. The belt-and-braces check is the exhaustive list of amended provisions in **Protocol No. 15, Article 1 (CETS No. 213)**. The text of CETS No. 213, Article 1 was not among the materials retrieved for this draft, so that cross-check is listed as a verification step in § 9 rather than asserted. It does not affect the answer: whatever else Protocol No. 15 changed, the operative sentence in § 1 is what the Protocol No. 15 consolidated text prints at Article 6 § 2.

---

## 4. Scope of what the quoted sentence itself says

The text is one sentence and it says three things: (i) the addressee is “everyone charged with a criminal offence”; (ii) the presumption is that such a person is “innocent”; (iii) it operates “until proved guilty according to law”. The sentence does **not** expressly state who bears the burden of proof, what standard of proof applies, or that silence is protected. Those propositions come from the Court's case law, not from the words of Article 6 § 2, and the module should attribute them accordingly (see § 6).

Related but distinct provisions in the same Article, for accurate cross-referencing:

> “1. In the determination of his civil rights and obligations or of any criminal charge against him, everyone is entitled to a fair and public hearing within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial tribunal established by law. […]”
>
> “3. Everyone charged with a criminal offence has the following minimum rights: (a) to be informed promptly, in a language which he understands and in detail, of the nature and cause of the accusation against him; (b) to have adequate time and facilities for the preparation of his defence; (c) to defend himself in person or through legal assistance of his own choosing or, if he has not sufficient means to pay for legal assistance, to be given it free when the interests of justice so require; (d) to examine or have examined witnesses against him and to obtain the attendance and examination of witnesses on his behalf under the same conditions as witnesses against him; (e) to have the free assistance of an interpreter if he cannot understand or speak the language used in court.”

---

## 5. Language versions

The English text in § 1 is the English authentic version as consolidated by the Council of Europe. The Convention was concluded in English and French, both texts equally authentic (Convention, concluding formula, Rome, 4 November 1950). The French rendering of Article 6 § 2, for a bilingual module, is:

> « 2. Toute personne accusée d'une infraction est présumée innocente jusqu'à ce que sa culpabilité ait été légalement établie. »

**Verification flag:** the French sentence above is reproduced here for the drafter's convenience and must be checked character-for-character against the ECHR's French consolidated version before it is published in any bilingual material. The English text in § 1 is the verified one; do not treat the two as equally verified on the strength of this draft. If the module is delivered in another official language of a member State, quote from that State's official translation only with a note identifying the translator and the date, and keep the English authentic text alongside it.

---

## 6. Case-law gloss — clearly labelled as gloss

The following propositions come from the European Court of Human Rights and are cited to the Court's own *Guide on Article 6 (criminal limb)*, which in turn cites the judgments. They should appear in the module as “what the Court has held”, never as “what Article 6 § 2 says”.

- **Core content of the presumption.** “Paragraph 2 of Article 6 embodies the principle of the presumption of innocence. It requires, inter alia, that: (1) when carrying out their duties, the members of a court should not start with the preconceived idea that the accused has committed the offence charged; (2) the burden of proof is on the prosecution, and (3) any doubt should benefit the accused.” — *Guide on Article 6 (criminal limb)*, § 362, citing **Barberà, Messegué and Jabardo v. Spain, 6 December 1988, § 77, Series A no. 146**.
- **Presumptions of fact or law are not prohibited in principle.** “A person's right in a criminal case to be presumed innocent and to require the prosecution to bear the onus of proving the allegations against him or her is not absolute, since presumptions of fact or of law operate in every criminal-law system and are not prohibited in principle by the Convention […]” — *Guide on Article 6 (criminal limb)*. The underlying authority is **Salabiaku v. France, 7 October 1988, § 28, Series A no. 141-A**; confirm the pin cite against HUDOC before it goes on a slide, as the Guide passage as retrieved does not print the citation.
- **Who counts as “charged”.** The Court has treated as “charged with a criminal offence”, and thus within Article 6 protection, a person arrested on suspicion of a criminal offence, a suspect questioned about his involvement in acts constituting a criminal offence, and a person questioned about suspected involvement irrespective of being formally treated as a witness, as well as a person formally charged under domestic procedure — *Guide on Article 6 (criminal limb)*, citing *inter alia* **Heaney and McGuinness v. Ireland, no. 34720/97, § 42, ECHR 2000-XII** and **Deweer v. Belgium, 27 February 1980, §§ 41–47, Series A no. 35**. Application numbers and report citations for the remaining cases listed in the Guide should be completed from HUDOC before publication.
- **The guarantee outlives the trial.** The presumption also protects persons acquitted or whose proceedings were discontinued from being treated by public officials and authorities as though they were in fact guilty — *Guide on Article 6 (criminal limb)*. It may be infringed not only by a judge or court but also by other public authorities — same source.

**Do-not-say list for the trainer** (each of these overstates the text):

1. Do not say Article 6 § 2 “places the burden of proof on the prosecution” as a matter of the text — that is the *Barberà* gloss.
2. Do not say Article 6 § 2 contains a right to silence or a privilege against self-incrimination — those are separate guarantees developed in the case law and should be cited separately.
3. Do not say the presumption is absolute — the Guide expressly records that it is not, because presumptions of fact or law are not prohibited in principle.
4. Do not present the sentence as a rule of evidence binding on non-criminal proceedings without checking the civil limb (Article 6 § 1) and the relevant case law.
5. Do not attribute the quoted words to Protocol No. 15, or describe them as “new” or “amended” — they are the unchanged Article 6 § 2 wording carried into the Protocol No. 15 consolidated text.

---

## 7. Jurisdictional framing for the module

The Convention obligation is territorial and jurisdictional in scope. Article 1, as amended by Protocol No. 15, reads:

> “The High Contracting Parties shall secure to everyone within their jurisdiction the rights and freedoms defined in Section I of this Convention.”

with the footnote: *“Text amended in accordance with the provisions of Protocol No. 15 (CETS No. 213) as from its entry into force on 1 August 2021.”* The module should therefore say that Article 6 § 2 binds Council of Europe member States Parties to the Convention and is interpreted by the European Court of Human Rights, and should not assume the same formulation governs in non-member jurisdictions or in domestic systems that protect the presumption by constitutional or statutory provision in different words.

---

## 8. Drop-in slide text (subject to attorney sign-off)

**Heading:** The presumption of innocence — Article 6 § 2 ECHR

**Verbatim box (quote exactly, in quotation marks, with the citation beneath):**
“Everyone charged with a criminal offence shall be presumed innocent until proved guilty according to law.”
*Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (ETS No. 5), Art. 6 § 2, as amended by Protocols Nos. 11, 14 and 15 (Protocol No. 15, CETS No. 213, in force 1 August 2021).*

**Gloss box (labelled “Court's interpretation, not the text”):** The European Court of Human Rights reads Article 6 § 2 as requiring that judges approach a case without a preconceived view of guilt, that the prosecution bear the burden of proof, and that doubt benefit the accused — *Barberà, Messegué and Jabardo v. Spain*, 6 December 1988, § 77, Series A no. 146.

---

## 9. Verification checklist before publication

1. Re-pull the ECHR consolidated English text and confirm the sentence in § 1 character-for-character, including “proved” and “according to law”.
2. Open **Protocol No. 15, Article 1 (CETS No. 213)** and confirm that Article 6 does not appear in the list of amended provisions — this converts the footnote-convention inference in § 3 into a direct citation.
3. Verify the French text in § 5 against the ECHR's French consolidated version.
4. Confirm the *Salabiaku* and remaining case citations in § 6 against HUDOC, completing application numbers and report citations.
5. Confirm the module's audience jurisdiction and, if it is a single member State, add the domestic provision implementing Article 6 § 2 with its own citation.

quotes.whole:
§ 3.11 Commencement of proceedings.




(a) Complaint.  Except as provided in § 3.13, an adjudicative proceeding is commenced when an affirmative vote is taken by the Commission to issue a complaint.






(b) Form of complaint.  The Commission's complaint shall contain the following:




(1) Recital of the legal authority and jurisdiction for institution of the proceeding, with specific designation of the statutory provisions alleged to have been violated;






(2) A clear and concise factual statement sufficient to inform each respondent with reasonable definiteness of the type of acts or practices alleged to be in violation of the law;






(3) Where practical, a form of order which the Commission has reason to believe should issue if the facts are found to be as alleged in the complaint; and





(4) Notice of the specific date, time and place for the evidentiary hearing. Unless a different date is determined by the Commission, the date of the evidentiary hearing shall be 5 months from the date of the administrative complaint in a proceeding in which the Commission, in an ancillary proceeding, has sought or is seeking relief pursuant to Section 13(b) of the FTC Act, 15 U.S.C. 53(b), and 8 months from the date of issuance of the administrative complaint in all other proceedings.

(b) Answer to application.
(1) Within 30 days after service of an application, complaint counsel may file an answer to the application. Unless complaint counsel requests an extension of time for filing or files a statement of intent to negotiate under paragraph (b)(2) of this section, failure to file an answer within the 30-day period may be treated as a consent to the award requested.

The filing of this statement shall extend the time for filing an answer for an additional 30 days, and further extensions may be granted by the Administrative Law Judge upon request by complaint counsel and the applicant.
(3) The answer shall explain in detail any objections to the award requested and identify the facts relied on in support of complaint counsel's position. If the answer is based on any alleged facts not already in the record of the proceeding, complaint counsel shall include with the answer either supporting affidavits or a request for further proceedings under paragraph (f) of this section.

quotes.whole: Within fourteen (14) days after completion of service of a Commission decision, any party may file with the Commission a petition for reconsideration of such decision, setting forth the relief desired and the grounds in support thereof. Any petition filed under this subsection must be confined to new questions raised by the decision or final order and upon which the petitioner had no opportunity to argue before the Commission. Any party desiring to oppose such a petition shall file an answer thereto within ten (10) days after service upon him of the petition. The filing of a petition for reconsideration shall not operate to stay the effective date of the decision or order or to toll the running of any statutory time period affecting such decision or order unless specifically so ordered by the Commission.

verdict.summary:
MEMORANDUM — COMBINED INTERVAL FROM SERVICE OF COMPLAINT TO SCHEDULING CONFERENCE, FTC PART 3 (SINGLE RESPONDENT)

Jurisdiction / procedure: Federal administrative adjudication before the Federal Trade Commission under 16 C.F.R. Part 3 (Rules of Practice for Adjudicative Proceedings), as in force on 2026-11-21. Not a court proceeding; the FTC's own rules supply the periods.

DRAFT FOR ATTORNEY REVIEW — NOT LEGAL ADVICE.

1. QUESTION PRESENTED
In a single-respondent FTC Part 3 adjudication governed by the version of Part 3 in force on 2026-11-21, where the respondent uses the entire answer period and the ALJ then uses the entire period allowed after the answer to hold the scheduling conference, what is the combined interval from service of the complaint to the conference, using only those two periods?

2. ANSWER
24 days.

3. GOVERNING AUTHORITY (quoted verbatim; primary sources cited in full)

(A) Answer period — 16 C.F.R. § 3.12(a) (2026): "A respondent shall file an answer within 14 days after being served with the complaint."
Source: Code of Federal Regulations, Title 16 (Commercial Practices), Chapter I, Subchapter A, Part 3, § 3.12(a), 2026 edition, U.S. Government Publishing Office, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2026-title16-vol1/xml/CFR-2026-title16-vol1-part3.xml (text also at https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-16/chapter-I/subchapter-A/part-3). Stated period: 14 days, running from service of the complaint.

(B) Conference period — 16 C.F.R. § 3.21(b) (2026): "Not later than 10 days after the answer is filed by the last answering respondent, the Administrative Law Judge shall hold a scheduling conference."
Source: 16 C.F.R. § 3.21(b) (2026), https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-16/part-3/section-3.21 and https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2026-title16-vol1/xml/CFR-2026-title16-vol1-part3.xml. Stated period: 10 days, running from the filing of the answer.

(C) Corroboration in Commission pleading practice: the Commission's Part 3 administrative complaint in In re Microsoft Corp./Activision Blizzard, Inc., FTC Docket No. 9412 (public version), states: "The Administrative Law Judge shall hold a prehearing scheduling conference not later than ten (10) days after the Respondents file their answers" and "the opportunity is afforded you to file with the Commission an answer to this complaint on or before the fourteenth (14th) day after service of it upon you." Source: https://www.ftc.gov/system/files/ftc_gov/pdf/D09412MicrosoftActivisionAdministrativeComplaintPublicVersionFinal.pdf. This confirms the two periods are 14 and 10 in the operative rule text; the rule, not the complaint form, controls.

4. COMPUTATION
Step 1 — Answer. Service of the complaint starts the § 3.12(a) clock. Full use of the period places the answer on the 14th day after service.
Step 2 — Conference. The § 3.21(b) clock starts on filing of the answer. Because there is one respondent, the sole respondent is the "last answering respondent"; no other answer can extend the trigger. Full use of the period places the conference on the 10th day after the answer.
Step 3 — Combine (sequential, not concurrent). 14 days + 10 days = 24 days after service.

Worked timeline (day of service excluded, the ordinary convention):
- Day 0 — complaint served.
- Day 14 — answer filed (last day of § 3.12(a) period).
- Day 24 — scheduling conference held (last day of § 3.21(b) period).
- Combined interval: 24 days.

5. DAY-COUNTING CONVENTION — WHAT IT DOES AND DOES NOT CHANGE
The two periods are stated in calendar days, not business days; neither § 3.12(a) nor § 3.21(b) says "business days." The 24-day total is the sum of the two stated periods and is invariant to the endpoint convention: counting the day of service as day 1 rather than day 0 shifts the calendar date of each step by one day but does not change 14 + 10 = 24. What the convention does affect is the calendar date on which the 24th day falls. If that date is a Saturday, Sunday, or federal holiday, a computation-of-time provision in Part 3 (16 C.F.R. § 3.7) would in the ordinary course roll the deadline to the next business day, producing an actual interval of 25 or 26 days. That roll is an application of a separate rule, not one of the two stated periods, and is therefore outside the figure requested. I did not retrieve the verified text of § 3.7 in this pass and do not quote or rely on it; it should be confirmed against the 2026 edition before any calendar date is fixed. The 24-day figure does not depend on it.

6. ASSUMPTIONS AND LIMITS ON THE FIGURE
(a) 24 days is a maximum under full use of both periods, not a typical or required timeline. If the respondent answers early, the § 3.21(b) trigger moves earlier and the interval shortens.
(b) Single respondent: no consolidation and no co-respondent whose later answer would reset the "last answering respondent" trigger.
(c) No extensions (16 C.F.R. § 3.21(c)(2) allows the ALJ, on good cause, to extend deadlines in the scheduling order), no motions to extend the answer, no amended complaint, no stay or tolling (compare the tolling provision for dispositive motions at 16 C.F.R. § 3.24(d)).
(d) Excluded by the "only those two periods" instruction, though they occur inside the same window: the § 3.21(a) meet-and-confer (no later than 5 days after the answers) and the § 3.21(c)(1) prehearing scheduling order (no later than 2 days after the conference). Adding them would overstate the requested figure.
(e) Service method: § 3.12(a) runs from service. If service was by a method that Part 3 treats as adding days, the answer date moves; the request fixes the answer period at its stated length, so no add-on is applied here.
(f) The date of the evidentiary hearing (5 months or 8 months from the complaint under 16 C.F.R. § 3.11(b)(4)) is unrelated to this calculation and does not constrain it.

7. CONCLUSION
Using only the two stated periods in 16 C.F.R. Part 3 as in force on 2026-11-21 — 14 days for the answer (§ 3.12(a)) and 10 days after the answer for the scheduling conference (§ 3.21(b)) — the combined interval from service of the complaint to the conference is 24 days.

quotes.whole: The aggregate turnover of an undertaking concerned within the meaning of this Regulation shall be calculated by adding together the respective turnovers of the following: (a) the undertaking concerned; (b) those undertakings in which the undertaking concerned, directly or indirectly: (i) owns more than half the capital or business assets, or (ii) has the power to exercise more than half the voting rights, or (iii) has the power to appoint more than half the members of the supervisory board, the administrative board or bodies legally representing the undertakings, or (iv) has the right to manage the undertakings' affairs; (c) those undertakings which have in the undertaking concerned the rights or powers listed in (b); (d) those undertakings in which an undertaking as referred to in (c) has the rights or powers listed in (b); (e) those undertakings in which two or more undertakings as referred to in (a) to (d) jointly have the rights or powers listed in (b).

verdict.summary:
DRAFT FOR ATTORNEY REVIEW — NOT LEGAL ADVICE

THRESHOLD MARGIN CALCULATION — ARTICLE 1(2)(a)–(b), COUNCIL REGULATION (EC) No 139/2004
Jurisdiction: European Union. These thresholds are specific to the EU merger control regime; they say nothing about any national merger control regime or any other jurisdiction.

1. SCOPE AND INSTRUCTION
This memorandum does one thing: it states, for each of the three recorded turnover amounts, the arithmetical amount by which that amount exceeds the corresponding threshold in Article 1(2)(a) and (b) of Council Regulation (EC) No 139/2004. It does not determine, and must not be read as determining, whether any concentration has a Community dimension. No such conclusion is drawn anywhere below (see §6).

2. THE RULE AND THE THRESHOLDS (primary source)
Council Regulation (EC) No 139/2004 of 20 January 2004 on the control of concentrations between undertakings (the EC Merger Regulation), OJ L 24, 29.1.2004, p. 1–22, Article 1(2), provides:

"2. A concentration has a Community dimension where:
(a) the combined aggregate worldwide turnover of all the undertakings concerned is more than EUR 5000 million; and
(b) the aggregate Community-wide turnover of each of at least two of the undertakings concerned is more than EUR 250 million,
unless each of the undertakings concerned achieves more than two-thirds of its aggregate Community-wide turnover within one and the same Member State."

Source: Regulation (EC) No 139/2004, Art. 1(2)(a)–(b), OJ L 24, 29.1.2004, p. 1; ELI http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2004/139/oj (text as published; the same wording appears in the English text at https://wipolex-res.wipo.int/edocs/lexdocs/laws/en/eu/eu104en.html).

Thresholds applied: (a) EUR 5,000 million, combined aggregate worldwide turnover of all undertakings concerned; (b) EUR 250 million, aggregate Community-wide turnover of each of at least two undertakings concerned.

Note the statutory comparator is "more than". Equality with the threshold does not satisfy it; every figure below is strictly above its threshold, so the margins are positive.

3. THE COMPUTATION
All amounts in EUR million, as recorded by the filing team, compared directly with the statutory figures. No currency conversion has been applied (all figures recorded in EUR).

Line 1 — Article 1(2)(a), combined aggregate worldwide turnover
  Recorded amount ......................... 5,400
  Threshold ............................... 5,000
  Excess (recorded − threshold) ........... 400
  Arithmetic .............................. 5,400 − 5,000 = 400; check 5,000 + 400 = 5,400

Line 2 — Article 1(2)(b), Community-wide turnover, undertaking 1
  Recorded amount ......................... 300
  Threshold ............................... 250
  Excess (recorded − threshold) ........... 50
  Arithmetic .............................. 300 − 250 = 50; check 250 + 50 = 300

Line 3 — Article 1(2)(b), Community-wide turnover, undertaking 2
  Recorded amount ......................... 275
  Threshold ............................... 250
  Excess (recorded − threshold) ........... 25
  Arithmetic .............................. 275 − 250 = 25; check 250 + 25 = 275

Summary of answers (EUR million):
  Combined worldwide turnover: exceeds EUR 5,000 million by EUR 400 million.
  Community-wide turnover, undertaking 1: exceeds EUR 250 million by EUR 50 million.
  Community-wide turnover, undertaking 2: exceeds EUR 250 million by EUR 25 million.

For reference only, the margins as a proportion of the threshold are 8.0% (400/5,000), 20.0% (50/250) and 10.0% (25/250). These percentages are descriptive; nothing in Article 1(2) turns on proportionality, only on the strict "more than" comparison.

4. ASSUMPTIONS ON WHICH THESE THREE FIGURES DEPEND (each is a point to confirm, not a finding)
(a) Threshold figures. The calculation uses the Article 1(2)(a)–(b) figures of EUR 5,000 million and EUR 250 million as they appear in the published text cited in §2. No amending or successor instrument was consulted; the figures should be re-verified against the consolidated version of Regulation 139/2004 in force on the date of the transaction. If either figure has changed, every margin above changes with it.
(b) Quality of the recorded amounts. The recorded amounts are taken as final turnover figures already calculated in accordance with Article 5 of Regulation 139/2004 — i.e. turnover of the undertakings concerned as aggregated under Article 5(4), net of intra-group and joint-venture sales as required by Article 5(5), and, where only parts of an undertaking are acquired, limited to the parts that are the subject of the concentration per Article 5(2) ("By way of derogation from paragraph 1, where the concentration consists of the acquisition of parts ... only the turnover relating to the parts which are the subject of the concentration shall be taken into account with regard to the seller or sellers."). Sources: Regulation (EC) No 139/2004, Art. 5(2), 5(4), 5(5). If the recorded figures are raw or provisional rather than Article 5-compliant, the margins must be recalculated after adjustment; a figure close to a threshold can move across it.
(c) Identity of the entities. The two Community-wide figures are assumed to correspond to two distinct undertakings concerned as that concept applies under the Regulation. Whether the recorded group perimeter matches the Article 5(4) aggregation perimeter is not verified here.
(d) Financial year and currency. The figures are assumed to relate to the same preceding financial year and to be expressed in euro, so that no conversion and no year-alignment adjustment is required. No exchange rate is applied.

5. WHAT THESE MARGINS DO AND DO NOT ESTABLISH
A positive margin means only that the recorded amount is greater than the statutory figure. It does not establish that the corresponding condition of Article 1(2) is legally satisfied, for at least four reasons that are outside this calculation: (i) Article 1(2) contains its own proviso — the two-thirds Member State rule — which is part of the operative test, not a separate defence; (ii) Article 1(2)(b) requires the condition to be met by "each of at least two" undertakings concerned, which depends on correctly identifying the undertakings concerned; (iii) Article 1(3) sets an alternative set of thresholds (EUR 2,500 million / EUR 100 million / EUR 25 million / EUR 100 million), which is not addressed here and on which no arithmetic is performed; and (iv) the referral mechanisms (Articles 4(5), 9 and 22) and the turnover rules of Article 5 are not applied here. Separately, the EUR 250 million figure that appears in Form CO point 3.5.2 is the EFTA-cooperation-case test for turnover in the territory of the EFTA States (Commission Regulation (EC) No 802/2004, Annex I (Form CO), points 3.3.1–3.3.3, 3.4 and 3.5.2, OJ L 133, 30.4.2004, p. 1, as amended) and is a different test from Article 1(2)(b); it is mentioned only so that it is not confused with the figure used above.

6. EXPRESS NON-DETERMINATION
No view is expressed, and none should be inferred, on whether the concentration has a Community dimension, whether Article 1(2) is satisfied or disapplied, whether the two-thirds proviso applies, whether Article 1(3) applies, or whether any notification, referral or filing obligation arises. The three figures in §3 are arithmetic differences and nothing more.

7. DEADLINES, NOTICE AND SERVICE
No deadline, notice period or service step is calculated or tracked here: the request supplies no trigger date (no signature, announcement, completion or notification date) and asks no timing question. If a trigger date is later supplied, the relevant periods would have to be counted under the provisions that create them (including Regulation 139/2004, Article 4(1) and the time-limit rules in Commission Regulation (EC) No 802/2004, Chapter III, including Article 24 on the definition of working days), and that would be a separate calculation.

8. SOURCES (full citations)
1. Council Regulation (EC) No 139/2004 of 20 January 2004 on the control of concentrations between undertakings (the EC Merger Regulation), OJ L 24, 29.1.2004, p. 1–22 — Article 1(2)(a)–(b) (thresholds and two-thirds proviso), Article 1(3) (alternative thresholds, referred to only to exclude), Article 5(2), 5(4), 5(5) (turnover calculation). ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2004/139/oj.
2. Commission Regulation (EC) No 802/2004 of 7 April 2004 implementing Council Regulation (EC) No 139/2004 on the control of concentrations between undertakings, OJ L 133, 30.4.2004, p. 1–39 (as amended) — Annex I (Form CO), points 2.4, 2.4.1, 3.3.1–3.3.3, 3.4, 3.5.2; Chapter III (time-limits) and Article 24 (definition of working days). ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2004/802/oj/eng.
3. English text of Regulation (EC) No 139/2004 reproduced at https://wipolex-res.wipo.int/edocs/lexdocs/laws/en/eu/eu104en.html (consulted for the Article 1(2) wording; the OJ text at source 1 is authoritative).

Draft prepared for review by a qualified attorney. Figures are arithmetic only and must be re-verified against the consolidated Regulation in force at the transaction date and against Article 5-compliant turnover data before any use.

findings.question:
1. A Member State has chosen the optional off-premises-contract exclusion in Directive 2011/83/EU at the maximum EUR 50 value. A consumer simultaneously concludes two contracts with related subjects, requiring payments of EUR 30 and EUR 25; what total is used for the threshold, and does that optional exclusion cover this pair on that basis?

quotes.whole:
Article 3(4) allows Member States not to apply the Directive to off-premises contracts, for which the payment to be made by the consumer does not exceed EUR 50 or a lower value as defined under national law. If a Member State chooses to use this regulatory choice, there is a risk that the Directive gets circumvented by traders who may decide to artificially split a single contract above the set threshold into several contracts. As explained in Recital 28: ‘[…] Where two or more contracts with related subjects are concluded at the same time by the consumer, the total cost thereof should be taken into account for the purpose of applying this threshold.’ This principle would apply to:
—
For example, selling each book of a trilogy under three separate contracts or selling a pair of earrings under two separate contracts at the same time.
For long-term contracts (subscriptions), the relevant amount for the application of this exception is the total amount that the consumer commits to pay when concluding the contract. i.e. the total amount of monthly instalments or charges over the agreed contractual period, including any ‘free’ periods.

quotes.whole:
pro rata temporis
.
It is only where the contract expressly provides that: (i) one or more of the services are to be provided in full from the beginning of the performance of the contract (ii) for a price which must be paid separately, that the full price for such a service should be taken into account in the calculation of the amount owed to the trader under Article 14(3) (134).
The Court further clarified in PE Digital that the test for the excessiveness of the compensation demanded by the trader is market-based. Pursuant to Article 14(3) of the CRD, read in the light of Recital 50 thereof, in this analysis account should be taken of the price of the service offered by the trader to other consumers under the same conditions and the price of an equivalent service supplied by other traders at the time of the conclusion of the contract (135).
Where services are provided under a sales contract, Recital 50 states the following: ‘[…] For contracts having as their object both goods and services, the rules provided for in this Directive on the return of goods should apply to the goods aspects and the
compensation regime for services should apply to the services aspects
’.

quotes.whole:
Article 3(4) allows Member States not to apply the Directive to off-premises contracts, for which the payment to be made by the consumer does not exceed EUR 50 or a lower value as defined under national law. If a Member State chooses to use this regulatory choice, there is a risk that the Directive gets circumvented by traders who may decide to artificially split a single contract above the set threshold into several contracts. As explained in Recital 28: ‘[…] Where two or more contracts with related subjects are concluded at the same time by the consumer, the total cost thereof should be taken into account for the purpose of applying this threshold.’ This principle would apply to:
—
For example, selling each book of a trilogy under three separate contracts or selling a pair of earrings under two separate contracts at the same time.
For long-term contracts (subscriptions), the relevant amount for the application of this exception is the total amount that the consumer commits to pay when concluding the contract. i.e. the total amount of monthly instalments or charges over the agreed contractual period, including any ‘free’ periods.

pro rata temporis
.
It is only where the contract expressly provides that: (i) one or more of the services are to be provided in full from the beginning of the performance of the contract (ii) for a price which must be paid separately, that the full price for such a service should be taken into account in the calculation of the amount owed to the trader under Article 14(3) (134).

Pursuant to Article 14(3) of the CRD, read in the light of Recital 50 thereof, in this analysis account should be taken of the price of the service offered by the trader to other consumers under the same conditions and the price of an equivalent service supplied by other traders at the time of the conclusion of the contract (135).

’.

quotes.whole: Certain exceptions from the right of withdrawal should exist, both for distance and off-premises contracts. A right of withdrawal could be inappropriate for example given the nature of particular goods or services. That is the case for example with wine supplied a long time after the conclusion of a contract of a speculative nature where the value is dependent on fluctuations in the market (‘vin en primeur’). The right of withdrawal should neither apply to goods made to the consumer’s specifications or which are clearly personalised such as tailor-made curtains, nor to the supply of fuel, for example, which is a good, by nature inseparably mixed with other items after delivery. The granting of a right of withdrawal to the consumer could also be inappropriate in the case of certain services where the conclusion of the contract implies the setting aside of capacity which, if a right of withdrawal were exercised, the trader may find difficult to fill. This would for example be the case where reservations are made at hotels or concerning holiday cottages or cultural or sporting events.
