verdict.summary:
# MEMORANDUM — DRAFT FOR ATTORNEY REVIEW

**This is a draft work product for review by a qualified attorney. It is not legal advice and must not be relied on by a client in its unreviewed form.**

**Subject:** Directive 2011/83/EU, Article 3(4) optional exclusion for low-value off-premises contracts (Member State option exercised at the EUR 50 maximum) — (i) what total is used for the threshold where a consumer simultaneously concludes two contracts with related subjects for EUR 30 and EUR 25, and (ii) whether the exclusion covers that pair on that basis.

**Jurisdiction:** European Union (Directive level). The Member State whose transposition governs is not identified in the instruction; the EU-level answer is given in Parts A–E and the Member-State-dependent points are isolated in Part F. A rule that holds at Directive level is not assumed to hold identically in every national transposition.

---

## PART A — ANSWERS

### A.1 (Ask 1) Total used for the threshold: **EUR 55**

The two prices are **aggregated**: EUR 30 + EUR 25 = **EUR 55**. The EUR 50 threshold is not applied contract-by-contract where two or more contracts with related subjects are concluded at the same time by the consumer. The aggregation rule is stated in Recital 28 of Directive 2011/83/EU:

> “Where two or more contracts with related subjects are concluded at the same time by the consumer, the total cost thereof should be taken into account for the purpose of applying this threshold.”

### A.2 (Ask 2) Does the optional exclusion cover this pair on that basis: **No**

Article 3(4) of Directive 2011/83/EU permits a Member State to disapply the Directive only to off-premises contracts “for which the payment to be made by the consumer **does not exceed EUR 50**”. The relevant payment on the aggregation rule is **EUR 55**, which **exceeds** EUR 50 by EUR 5. The exclusion is therefore **unavailable for the pair**, and the consequence is not that one contract is excluded and the other is not — it is that the exclusion cannot be relied on at all, so **both** contracts remain within the Directive and within the national transposition, carrying the full Chapter III information and withdrawal regime.

**Direction of the test (worth stating expressly in any advice):** “does not exceed” means ≤ EUR 50. A pair totalling exactly EUR 50 would fall inside the exclusion. EUR 55 does not.

### A.3 Worked threshold table

| Unit of assessment | Payment | Cumulative total | Exceeds EUR 50? | Exclusion available? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Contract 1 alone | EUR 30 | EUR 30 | No | Yes (if assessed alone) |
| Contract 2 alone | EUR 25 | EUR 25 | No | Yes (if assessed alone) |
| **Pair, aggregated (correct test)** | **EUR 30 + EUR 25** | **EUR 55** | **Yes** | **No** |

**Why the aggregation rule is outcome-determinative here.** Both legs are individually below the ceiling. Without aggregation, the trader would escape the Directive on **both** contracts; with aggregation, the trader escapes on **neither**. This is precisely the contract-splitting pattern the rule exists to defeat, and the pair should be advised on that footing.

---

## PART B — PRIMARY SOURCES RELIED ON (full citations)

**B.1 Directive 2011/83/EU.** Directive 2011/83/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 25 October 2011 on consumer rights, amending Council Directive 93/13/EEC and Directive 1999/44/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council and repealing Council Directive 85/577/EEC and Directive 97/7/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council, OJ L 304, 22.11.2011, p. 64–88; ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2011/83/oj (consolidated text consulted on EUR-Lex, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2011/83/oj).

Provisions relied on: Article 3(1), Article 3(4), Article 3(5), Article 4, Article 6(1)(e), Article 13(1), Article 15(1); Recital 28.

**B.2 European Commission guidance (persuasive, not binding).** European Commission, *Guidance on the interpretation and application of Directive 2011/83/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council on consumer rights*, OJ C 525, 29.12.2021, p. 1 — section 1.8, “Possible exemption of low value off-premises contracts”. Copy consulted: Publications Office CELLAR, http://publications.europa.eu/resource/cellar/a5f87ef3-6849-11ec-9136-01aa75ed71a1.0006.03/DOC_1. **[Action for reviewing attorney: confirm the OJ C 525 pagination against the Official Journal before this citation is used in a filed document; the CELLAR URI is the copy actually consulted.]**

**B.3 Case law on interpretive method (cited for method, not for the aggregation rule itself — see C.6).**
- Case C-14/83 *Sabine von Colson and Elisabeth Kamann v Land Nordrhein-Westfalen* [1984] ECR 1891 (duty of conforming interpretation of national law implementing a directive).
- Case C-106/89 *Marleasing SA v La Comercial Internacional de Alimentación SA* [1990] ECR I-4135 (conforming interpretation extends to national law adopted to implement a directive and to pre-existing national law).
- Case C-322/88 *Salvatore Grimaldi v Fonds des maladies professionnelles* [1989] ECR 4407 (recommendations and guidance lack binding force but are persuasive interpretive material for national courts).
- Case C-162/97 *Criminal proceedings against Gunnar Nilsson and others* [1998] ECR I-7477, para. 54 (a preamble/recital has no binding legal force of its own and cannot be used to derogate from the operative provisions — cited here **against** the aggregation argument as well as for it; see C.5).

**B.4 National transposition.** Not identified in the instruction. See Part F for exactly what must be obtained and checked.

---

## PART C — ANALYSIS

### C.1 The two-limb structure of Article 3(4)

Article 3(4) provides, verbatim:

> “Member States may decide not to apply this Directive or not to maintain or introduce corresponding national provisions to off-premises contracts for which the payment to be made by the consumer does not exceed EUR 50. Member States may define a lower value in their national legislation.”

Two features matter.

1. **It is a Member State option, not a trader defence arising automatically.** The exclusion operates only if, and to the extent that, the Member State has exercised it. The instruction fixes the premise that the Member State has exercised it at the EUR 50 maximum, so the ceiling to be applied is EUR 50 and no lower national figure applies.
2. **It is a total disapplication, not a partial one.** The text reads “not to apply **this Directive**”, not “not to apply the withdrawal right”. If the exclusion applies, the Directive as a whole does not apply to the contract and the consumer’s position is governed by national general law. If it does not apply, the Directive applies in full. There is no intermediate state. This matters to how the answer is framed: the question “does the exclusion cover the pair” is a scope question, not a question about which individual rights survive.

### C.2 The aggregation rule

Recital 28, verbatim:

> “In order to avoid administrative burden being placed on traders, Member States may decide not to apply this Directive where goods or services of a minor value are sold off-premises. The monetary threshold should be established at a sufficiently low level as to exclude only purchases of small significance. Member States should be allowed to define this value in their national legislation provided that it does not exceed EUR 50. **Where two or more contracts with related subjects are concluded at the same time by the consumer, the total cost thereof should be taken into account for the purpose of applying this threshold.**”

The Commission’s guidance reads the same rule and identifies its anti-circumvention purpose in terms, verbatim:

> “Article 3(4) allows Member States not to apply the Directive to off-premises contracts, for which the payment to be made by the consumer does not exceed EUR 50 or a lower value as defined under national law. If a Member State chooses to use this regulatory choice, there is a risk that the Directive gets circumvented by traders who may decide to artificially split a single contract above the set threshold into several contracts. As explained in Recital 28: ‘[…] Where two or more contracts with related subjects are concluded at the same time by the consumer, the total cost thereof should be taken into account for the purpose of applying this threshold.’ This principle would apply to: — For example, selling each book of a trilogy under three separate contracts or selling a pair of earrings under two separate contracts at the same time.”

The two worked examples — a trilogy split into three book contracts, and a pair of earrings split into two contracts — are the closest guidance-level analogy to a pair of related contracts priced at EUR 30 and EUR 25 concluded at the same time. The guidance also confirms the measurement rule for continuing contracts: “For long-term contracts (subscriptions), the relevant amount for the application of this exception is the total amount that the consumer commits to pay when concluding the contract. i.e. the total amount of monthly instalments or charges over the agreed contractual period, including any ‘free’ periods.” That is not needed on the assumed facts (single payments), but it should be checked if either contract has a recurring element.

### C.3 The operative test to be applied

Two cumulative conditions, both drawn from the recital text:

**(a) “concluded at the same time”.** The instruction assumes simultaneity (“simultaneously concludes … at the same time in the course of a single commercial transaction”). Treat as satisfied on the assumed facts. If it were contested, the relevant evidence is the timing of offer and acceptance, whether a single visit/occasion produced both, and whether the trader presented them as one transaction.

**(b) “contracts with related subjects”.** The Directive does not define this phrase in Article 2. It is not a term of art with a settled autonomous meaning. The Commission’s examples (the trilogy; the earrings) indicate that the relation is one of shared commercial object — goods or services forming a set, collection or single economic purchase, or obligations that are interdependent. Indicators an attorney should test on the file: same trader; same occasion and same place; a single commercial purpose from the consumer’s standpoint; interdependence of the obligations (performance of one is pointless or impaired without the other); presentation as a package or with cross-referenced terms; a single payment, single delivery or single invoice; and whether the consumer would reasonably have understood the transaction as one purchase.

On the instruction’s own characterisation (“two contracts with related subjects”), condition (b) is treated as given. **This is the single factual point on which the whole answer pivots** — if the two contracts are genuinely unrelated (independent purchases that happened to be made at the same time from the same trader), aggregation does not apply, each contract is assessed at EUR 30 and EUR 25 respectively, both fall below EUR 50, and the exclusion covers both. That is the opposite result, and the reviewing attorney should not let the characterisation pass unexamined.

### C.4 Application to the facts

- Condition (a): satisfied (assumed simultaneity).
- Condition (b): satisfied (instruction characterises the contracts as with related subjects; the trilogy/earrings analogies in the Commission guidance support it).
- Therefore the threshold is tested on the **total cost**: EUR 30 + EUR 25 = **EUR 55**.
- EUR 55 > EUR 50. The condition in Article 3(4) — payment “does not exceed EUR 50” — is **not** met.
- **The optional exclusion does not cover the pair.**

### C.5 Consequence of the exclusion not applying

Because Article 3(4) is an all-or-nothing disapplication (C.1), the failure of the exclusion means the Directive and its national transposition apply to **both** contracts, including:

- the pre-contractual information duties in Article 6, including the total price inclusive of taxes and additional charges under Article 6(1)(e);
- the withdrawal regime in Articles 9 to 16 (the 14-day period and its consequences), subject to any Article 16 exception that independently applies on the facts;
- Article 13(1) reimbursement: “The trader shall reimburse all payments received from the consumer, including, if applicable, the costs of delivery without undue delay and in any event not later than 14 days from the day on which he is informed of the consumer’s decision to withdraw from the contract in accordance with Article 11.”
- **A practical point the file should be checked for:** if one of the two contracts is ancillary to the other (credit, insurance, installation, extended warranty), Article 15(1) provides that on withdrawal from the main distance or off-premises contract “any ancillary contracts shall be automatically terminated, without any costs for the consumer, except as provided for in Article 13(2) and in Article 14 of this Directive.” On a related-subjects pair this is a live possibility and materially changes the remedy.

### C.6 Counter-arguments and where the authority is thin

Stated plainly, because the reviewing attorney needs to know the weak joints.

**(i) The aggregation rule is in a recital, not in the operative text.** Article 3(4) contains no aggregation sentence. A trader could argue that Article 3(4) as enacted tests “the payment to be made by the consumer” under each contract, and that Recital 28 cannot supply a condition absent from the operative provision. The counter is that recitals are a recognised interpretive aid and that Article 3(4) must be read in the light of the objective Recital 28 articulates (excluding only “purchases of small significance” and preventing circumvention by splitting). The counter-counter is *Nilsson* (C-162/97, para. 54): a preamble has no binding force and cannot be relied on to derogate from the operative provisions. **This is a genuine argument and the answer is not free from doubt at Directive level.** In practice it is resolved less by EU-law argument than by the national transposition, which in most Member States that used the option reproduces the aggregation rule (Part F).

**(ii) No CJEU judgment on the aggregation rule was located.** The instruction’s research returned the Directive text, the Commission guidance and national implementing material, but no Court of Justice ruling construing “contracts with related subjects” or the aggregation mechanism. The authority at EU level is therefore a recital plus non-binding Commission guidance. The guidance is expressly persuasive only (*Grimaldi*, C-322/88). **Do not present the aggregation rule to a court as settled CJEU doctrine; present it as the Directive’s stated rule, reinforced by effet utile and by the national transposition.**

**(iii) The national transposition is unidentified.** This is the largest gap. If the Member State’s implementing provision reproduces the aggregation sentence, the answer is straightforward at national level and the Recital 28 debate is academic. If the implementing provision is silent, the consumer’s route is conforming interpretation (*von Colson*, C-14/83; *Marleasing*, C-106/89) — reading the national provision in the light of Article 3(4) and Recital 28 — which is a strong but not guaranteed route, and which cannot be used to interpret national law *contra legem*. See Part F.

**(iv) National general contract law is expressly preserved.** Article 3(5): “This Directive shall not affect national general contract law such as the rules on the validity, formation or effect of a contract, in so far as general contract law aspects are not regulated in this Directive.” Whether the two contracts form a single indivisible transaction, or whether splitting them is an abuse of right or a simulation, is a question of national civil law and may independently reinforce (or complicate) the Recital 28 analysis. It is not displaced by the Directive, and it should be pleaded alongside rather than instead of the aggregation argument.

**(v) Level of harmonisation.** Article 4 forbids Member States from maintaining or introducing divergent provisions “unless otherwise provided for in this Directive”. Article 3(4) is such an “otherwise provided for”. This confirms that the exclusion’s scope is fixed by the Directive’s terms and is not open to a Member State to widen by, for example, permitting per-contract assessment without aggregation — a further support for reading Article 3(4) subject to Recital 28.

### C.7 Measurement of “the payment to be made by the consumer”

Article 3(4) refers to “the payment to be made by the consumer”, not to “the price”; Recital 28 refers to “the total cost thereof”. Both formulations point to the total amount payable rather than a net figure. The instruction assumes the EUR 30 and EUR 25 figures are inclusive of any relevant charges for threshold purposes; that assumption is adopted. If it is wrong, the figures must be restated on a total-cost basis before the threshold is applied — delivery, booking and ancillary charges that the consumer must pay all count.

---

## PART D — ASSUMPTIONS (each to be confirmed, not treated as fact)

1. The Member State validly exercised the Article 3(4) option and set the exclusion at the EUR 50 maximum (not a lower figure).
2. The two contracts were concluded at the same time in the course of a single commercial transaction.
3. The contracts are “with related subjects” within the meaning of Recital 28.
4. The EUR 30 and EUR 25 figures are the total payments to be made by the consumer, inclusive of taxes and any additional charges.
5. Both contracts are off-premises contracts within Article 2(8) and neither falls within an Article 3(3) exclusion or an Article 16 exception on grounds independent of value.
6. Both amounts are denominated in euro; no currency conversion is required.
7. The contracts were concluded at a time when the transposing law in force included the option.

If assumption 3 fails, the answer to Ask 2 reverses (see C.3). If assumption 1 fails because the national figure is lower than EUR 50, the answer to Ask 2 does not change (a lower ceiling is exceeded a fortiori by EUR 55), though the analysis must cite the correct national figure.

---

## PART E — VERIFICATION CHECKLIST BEFORE THIS DRAFT IS USED

1. Obtain and quote the exact national implementing provision corresponding to Article 3(4), in the version in force at the date of conclusion.
2. Confirm whether that provision contains the aggregation sentence, and quote it verbatim if so.
3. Identify any national case law on contract-splitting or on “related subjects”/“related subject matter”.
4. Confirm the national threshold figure (EUR 50 or lower) and that it is not index-linked.
5. Confirm the contracts are off-premises contracts and that no Article 3(3) or Article 16 exclusion applies independently.
6. Confirm the total-cost figures (taxes and charges included).
7. Confirm the date of conclusion against the transposition’s entry into force.
8. Confirm the OJ citation of the Commission guidance (B.2).
9. Check whether either contract is ancillary to the other for Article 15(1) purposes.

---

## PART F — WHAT IS MEMBER-STATE-DEPENDENT (and what is not)

The following **do not** depend on the Member State: the arithmetic (EUR 30 + EUR 25 = EUR 55); the fact that EUR 55 exceeds EUR 50; the text of Article 3(4) and Recital 28; and the conclusion that, on the Directive’s own stated rule, the exclusion is unavailable for the pair.

The following **do** depend on the Member State and must be confirmed before advice is given:

- **The exact wording of the transposition.** Whether the aggregation sentence was carried into binding national law, and in what terms.
- **The legal test for “related subjects” in that jurisdiction.** No settled autonomous EU meaning exists (C.3); national courts may have supplied criteria.
- **The interaction with national general contract law** (Article 3(5)) — indivisibility, simulation, abuse of right, and any national rule against contract-splitting.
- **Currency conversion**, if either contract is not in euro; the Directive fixes EUR 50 and does not itself prescribe a conversion method.
- **Remedies and consequences** of the Directive applying — procedural and remedial detail is national.

If the transposition is silent on aggregation, the argument to run is: Article 3(4) must be construed in the light of Recital 28 and of the anti-circumvention objective it states; Article 4 precludes a divergent national widening of the exclusion; and the national provision must be interpreted conformably (*von Colson*, C-14/83; *Marleasing*, C-106/89). Flag the *Nilsson* limitation (C.6(i)) candidly in any advice.

---

## PART G — SOURCE TABLE

| Ref | Source | Status | Used for |
|---|---|---|---|
| B.1 | Directive 2011/83/EU, OJ L 304, 22.11.2011, p. 64–88, ELI http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2011/83/oj | Binding EU law | Art. 3(4) option and ceiling; Recital 28 aggregation rule; Art. 3(5), 4, 6(1)(e), 13(1), 15(1) |
| B.2 | Commission Guidance, OJ C 525, 29.12.2021, p. 1, §1.8 | Non-binding; persuasive | Anti-circumvention rationale; trilogy and earrings examples; subscription measurement |
| B.3 | C-14/83 *von Colson*; C-106/89 *Marleasing*; C-322/88 *Grimaldi*; C-162/97 *Nilsson* | Binding (first two, method); persuasive/limiting (last two) | Conforming interpretation; status of guidance; limits of recitals |
| B.4 | National transposition | Binding, unidentified | Governs the final answer — see Part F |

---

*Prepared as a draft for review by a qualified attorney. Not legal advice. Every statement of law above is tied to the source cited; where authority is thin or contested (C.6), that is stated rather than smoothed over.*

verdict.summary:
DRAFT FOR ATTORNEY REVIEW — NOT LEGAL ADVICE

MEMORANDUM

TO: Supervising Attorney (manual revision)
FROM: Legal Research
RE: Status of the "Appendix of Forms" to the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure under the rules as amended to December 1, 2025; effective date of the change; consequences for a 2014 litigation manual
JURISDICTION: United States — procedure in the U.S. district courts under the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure (Fed. R. Civ. P. 1). State-court procedural analogues are outside this memo; a rule stated here for the federal courts is not assumed to hold in any state.

=====================================================================
I. QUESTIONS PRESENTED
=====================================================================

1. [Constraint] Whether the analysis below is stated against the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure as amended to December 1, 2025.
2. What is the status, in those rules, of the Appendix of Forms to which a 2014 litigation manual still directs users?
3. When did that change take effect?

=====================================================================
II. SHORT ANSWERS
=====================================================================

1. Yes — every statement below is taken from the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure as amended to and including December 1, 2025 (Judicial Conference of the United States, Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, Foreword, Dec. 1, 2025).

2. ABROGATED. The Appendix of Forms is no longer a component of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure. It was not renamed, suspended, relocated into the rule text, or replaced in place; it was abrogated in its entirety, together with Rule 84 — the rule that had given the forms operative effect. The rules now carry the abrogation parenthetical in the place where the Appendix stood: "XII. APPENDIX OF FORMS [Abrogated (Apr. 29, 2015, eff. Dec. 1, 2015).]" and "Rule 84. [Abrogated (Apr. 29, 2015, eff. Dec. 1, 2015).]"

3. DECEMBER 1, 2015 (2015-12-01). The amendments were adopted by the Supreme Court by order dated April 29, 2015, transmitted to Congress by the Chief Justice the same day (575 U.S. 1055; Cong. Rec., vol. 161, pt. 5, p. 6139, Ex. Comm. 1373; H. Doc. 114-33), and became effective December 1, 2015 under the Rules Enabling Act, 28 U.S.C. §§ 2072, 2074.

=====================================================================
III. GOVERNING AUTHORITY (full citations)
=====================================================================

Primary:

1. Order of the Supreme Court of the United States, April 29, 2015, adopting amendments to the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, 575 U.S. 1055 (2015); transmitted to Congress by the Chief Justice April 29, 2015; Cong. Rec., vol. 161, pt. 5, p. 6139, Ex. Comm. 1373; H. Doc. 114-33. [Citation as given in the official pamphlet's historical note; the order's text was not in the materials reviewed — see § VII.]

2. Fed. R. Civ. P. 84 (abrogated Apr. 29, 2015, eff. Dec. 1, 2015).

3. Appendix of Forms, Fed. R. Civ. P., Title XII (abrogated Apr. 29, 2015, eff. Dec. 1, 2015).

4. 28 U.S.C. § 2072 (Rules Enabling Act — power to prescribe rules of procedure; rules "shall not abridge, enlarge or modify any substantive right").

5. 28 U.S.C. § 2074 (congressional review; transmittal not later than May 1 of the year in which a rule is to take effect; rule takes effect no earlier than December 1 of that year unless otherwise provided by law).

6. Fed. R. Civ. P. 86(a) (Effective Dates — rules and amendments take effect at the time specified by the Supreme Court, subject to 28 U.S.C. § 2074).

7. Fed. R. Civ. P. 83 (Rules by District Courts; Judge's Directives) — governs local rules and local forms, the remaining source of court-specific form requirements.

8. Judicial Conference of the United States, Committee on Rules of Practice and Procedure, Federal Rules of Civil Procedure (as amended to December 1, 2025), Foreword (Dec. 1, 2025) and Historical Note, https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-civil-procedure.pdf (fetched 2026-11-23; sha256 bd8705fc038d).

9. Federal Judicial Center, Amendments to the Federal Rules of Practice and Procedure 2015—Civil Rules Redline (Dec. 1, 2015), https://www.fjc.gov/content/309299/amendments-federal-rules-practice-and-procedure-2015-civil-rules-redline (fetched 2026-11-23; sha256 7d0b770c9abc).

10. Federal Judicial Center, Amendments to the Federal Rules of Practice and Procedure 2015—Transmittal to Congress (Apr. 29, 2015), https://www.fjc.gov/content/309296/rules-amendments-2015-congress-transmittal (fetched 2026-11-23; sha256 6d90fc6fa153).

Secondary / corroborative only:

11. Cornell Legal Information Institute, Federal Rules of Civil Procedure (as amended to December 1, 2025), https://www.law.cornell.edu/rules/frcp (fetched 2026-11-23; sha256 803b4574ea1a). Used solely to corroborate the abrogation parentheticals; not relied on as authority.

=====================================================================
IV. ANALYSIS
=====================================================================

A. What the Appendix of Forms was, and what it did

Since the original rules took effect on September 16, 1938, the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure carried an Appendix of Forms — simplified model pleadings and process papers appended to the rules themselves as Title XII. The forms were given operative effect by Rule 84. As restyled effective December 1, 2007, the Appendix contained Forms 1 through 82: the 2007 restyling converted the original Forms 1 through 35 into restyled Forms 1 through 82. Judicial Conference, Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, Historical Note (as amended to Dec. 1, 2025) ("Forms 1 through 35 were amended to become restyled Forms 1 through 82").

[Verification flag: former Rule 84 as restyled in 2007 read, in substance, that "[t]he forms in the Appendix suffice under these rules and illustrate the simplicity and brevity that these rules contemplate." That language is NOT in the December 1, 2025 pamphlet (which carries only the abrogation parenthetical), so it must be confirmed against a 2014 print of the Rules before it is quoted in any published annotation. See § VII, item 1.]

B. The 2015 amendment: two distinct abrogations

The 2015 package did two separate things that are frequently conflated:

(i) it abrogated Rule 84; and
(ii) it abrogated the Appendix of Forms (Forms 1 through 82).

Both are stated in the official pamphlet's historical note, verbatim: "Additional amendments were adopted by the Court by order dated April 29, 2015, transmitted to Congress by the Chief Justice on the same day (575 U.S. 1055; Cong. Rec., vol. 161, pt. 5, p. 6139, Ex. Comm. 1373; H. Doc. 114-33), and became effective December 1, 2015. The amendments affected Rules 1, 4, 16, 26, 30, 31, 33, 34, 37, and 55, abrogated Rule 84, and abrogated the Appendix of Forms (Forms 1 through 82)." (Judicial Conference, Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, Historical Note (as amended to Dec. 1, 2025).)

The Federal Judicial Center states the same in its own words: "Amendments to the following Federal Rules of Civil Procedure became effective on December 1, 2015: 1, 4, 16, 26, 30, 31, 33, 34, 37, and 55. Rule 84 and the Appendix of Forms were abrogated." (FJC, 2015—Civil Rules Redline.) And in the transmittal package: "Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 84 and the Appendix of Forms were abrogated." (FJC, 2015—Transmittal to Congress.)

The distinction matters practically: abrogating the Appendix alone would have removed the forms while leaving Rule 84's safe harbor pointing at nothing; abrogating Rule 84 alone would have left forms with no rule-based effect. The 2015 package did both, so neither the forms nor the safe harbor survives.

C. Effective-date mechanics

Under 28 U.S.C. § 2074, a rule prescribed under § 2072 must be transmitted to Congress not later than May 1 of the year in which it is to become effective, and takes effect no earlier than December 1 of that year unless Congress provides otherwise. Rule 86(a) confirms that the rules and amendments "take effect at the time specified by the Supreme Court, subject to 28 U.S.C. § 2074."

The timeline is therefore:
- April 29, 2015 — Supreme Court order adopting the amendments; transmission to Congress by the Chief Justice the same day (within the May 1 window).
- December 1, 2015 — effective date, the earliest date § 2074 permits for a 2015 transmittal.

No statute deferring, modifying, or rejecting the 2015 package appears in the materials reviewed, and the official 2025 pamphlet and the FJC both record December 1, 2015 as the operative date. If the file requires negative confirmation of congressional action, that check is a search of the Statutes at Large / Congress.gov for 2015 legislation under § 2074; it is not a gap in the answer, only a belt-and-braces step.

D. Status as of December 1, 2025 — no resurrection

The rules as amended to December 1, 2025 contain no Appendix of Forms. The current official text shows the abrogation in place, at both locations:
- "Rule 84. [Abrogated (Apr. 29, 2015, eff. Dec. 1, 2015).]" (Judicial Conference, Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, Title XI (as amended to Dec. 1, 2025).)
- "XII. APPENDIX OF FORMS [Abrogated (Apr. 29, 2015, eff. Dec. 1, 2015).]" (same; corroborated at Cornell LII, Federal Rules of Civil Procedure index (as amended to Dec. 1, 2025), which lists "Rule 84. Abrogated, eff. Dec. 1, 2015" and "XII. APPENDIX OF FORMS [Abrogated (Apr. 29, 2015, eff. Dec. 1, 2015).]")

Nothing between 2015 and 2025 re-established the Appendix; the 2025 pamphlet continues to carry the 2015 parentheticals, and Title XIII (Supplemental Rules for Admiralty or Maritime Claims and Asset Forfeiture Actions) follows directly.

One nuance the manual must not blur: forms as a category did not disappear. The Foreword to the December 1, 2025 pamphlet still describes the document as containing "the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure together with forms, as amended to December 1, 2025." What disappeared is the Appendix of Forms as a titled component of the Rules and Rule 84's statement that those forms "suffice." Current forms are published by the Judicial Conference / the federal judiciary's official forms program (uscourts.gov) and in the pamphlet's forms material, not as an Appendix to the Rules.

E. Consequences for the 2014 manual — three separate defects

A 2014 manual's direction to "the Appendix of Forms" was accurate when written and became obsolete on December 1, 2015. The manual now contains three defects, not one:

1. Dead citation target. There is no Appendix of Forms in the rules; a reader following the instruction finds an abrogation parenthetical.
2. Dead safe harbor. Former Rule 84 told parties that use of an Appendix form "suffices." That assurance is gone; a litigant cannot rely on form-compliance as a defense to a pleading or process challenge. The content requirements that the forms illustrated now live in the rule text itself — e.g., the mandatory contents of a summons are set out in Fed. R. Civ. P. 4(a) ("A summons must: ..."), not in a form.
3. Stale numbering. The manual's form numbers reflect the 2007 restyling (Forms 1 through 82, effective December 1, 2007), a numbering scheme that the 2015 abrogation then superseded. Any cross-reference to a numbered Appendix form is doubly out of date.

Replacement guidance for the manual's readers: (a) use the current official forms published by the federal judiciary (uscourts.gov) — e.g., the Summons in a Civil Action (Form AO 440) and the notice/waiver-of-service forms (AO 398/399) [verify current form numbers before publication — § VII, item 3]; (b) check the district's local rules and local forms, which remain a valid source of form requirements under Fed. R. Civ. P. 83; and (c) do not treat any form, current or former, as establishing sufficiency as a matter of law.

[Analysis flag: the interaction between the loss of the Rule 84 safe harbor and federal pleading standards is my reading, not a holding. If the manual discusses pleading sufficiency, pair the annotation with Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007), and Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009), each cited in full and independently verified before publication.]

F. Where the authority is thin or conflicting

- The operative primary source is the Supreme Court's April 29, 2015 order. The materials reviewed supply its citation (575 U.S. 1055) and its effect through the official pamphlet's historical note and the FJC's two publications; the order's own text was not in the file. For a publication-grade annotation, pull the order.
- The 2015 Advisory Committee Note explaining the abrogation (its rationale and any statement about continued availability of forms) was not in the materials reviewed. Do not paraphrase it until obtained.
- The exact title and placement of the current forms material in the official pamphlet is confirmed only at the level of the Foreword's phrase "together with forms"; the forms section itself was not examined. State the point at that level of generality or verify.
- Cornell LII is a reliable index but is secondary; it is used here only to corroborate the parentheticals, which appear identically in the official pamphlet.
- No conflict in the authority reviewed: the pamphlet, the FJC redline, and the FJC transmittal package agree on both the fact of abrogation and the December 1, 2015 effective date.

=====================================================================
V. READY-TO-PASTE ANNOTATION FOR THE MANUAL
=====================================================================

"EDITOR'S NOTE (current through Fed. R. Civ. P. as amended Dec. 1, 2025): The Appendix of Forms no longer exists. The Supreme Court's order of April 29, 2015 (575 U.S. 1055; transmitted to Congress Apr. 29, 2015; H. Doc. 114-33) abrogated both Rule 84 and the Appendix of Forms (Forms 1 through 82), effective December 1, 2015. The rules now read: 'Rule 84. [Abrogated (Apr. 29, 2015, eff. Dec. 1, 2015).]' and 'XII. APPENDIX OF FORMS [Abrogated (Apr. 29, 2015, eff. Dec. 1, 2015).]' Any reference in this chapter to a numbered Appendix form, and any reliance on the former Rule 84 statement that the forms 'suffice,' is obsolete. Use the current official forms published by the federal judiciary (uscourts.gov), together with any forms required by the district's local rules under Fed. R. Civ. P. 83. Form numbers cited in the 2014 text reflect the 2007 restyling and are superseded."

=====================================================================
VI. SOURCES, IN FULL
=====================================================================

1. Order of the Supreme Court of the United States, Apr. 29, 2015, 575 U.S. 1055 (2015) (adopting amendments to the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure); Cong. Rec., vol. 161, pt. 5, p. 6139, Ex. Comm. 1373; H. Doc. 114-33.
2. Fed. R. Civ. P. 84 (abrogated Apr. 29, 2015, eff. Dec. 1, 2015).
3. Fed. R. Civ. P., Title XII, Appendix of Forms (abrogated Apr. 29, 2015, eff. Dec. 1, 2015).
4. Fed. R. Civ. P. 4(a), 83, 86.
5. 28 U.S.C. §§ 2072, 2074.
6. Judicial Conference of the United States, Committee on Rules of Practice and Procedure, Federal Rules of Civil Procedure (as amended to Dec. 1, 2025), Foreword and Historical Note, https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-civil-procedure.pdf.
7. Federal Judicial Center, Amendments to the Federal Rules of Practice and Procedure 2015—Civil Rules Redline (Dec. 1, 2015), https://www.fjc.gov/content/309299/amendments-federal-rules-practice-and-procedure-2015-civil-rules-redline.
8. Federal Judicial Center, Amendments to the Federal Rules of Practice and Procedure 2015—Transmittal to Congress (Apr. 29, 2015), https://www.fjc.gov/content/309296/rules-amendments-2015-congress-transmittal.
9. Cornell Legal Information Institute, Federal Rules of Civil Procedure (as amended to Dec. 1, 2025), https://www.law.cornell.edu/rules/frcp (corroborative only).

=====================================================================
VII. VERIFICATION CHECKLIST BEFORE PUBLICATION
=====================================================================

1. Confirm the pre-2015 text of Rule 84 against a 2014 print of the Rules (for the word "suffice").
2. Obtain the text of the April 29, 2015 Supreme Court order (575 U.S. 1055) and the 2015 Advisory Committee Note to the abrogation of Rule 84 and the Appendix of Forms; add the Note's rationale if the annotation will explain "why."
3. Confirm current official form numbers and titles on uscourts.gov (AO 440, AO 398/399) before naming them.
4. Confirm no 2015 Act of Congress deferred or modified the package under 28 U.S.C. § 2074 (Statutes at Large / Congress.gov).
5. If any state-court procedure is discussed in the same chapter, research that jurisdiction separately; nothing here is offered as a statement of state law.
6. Attorney review and sign-off; this memorandum is a draft and is not legal advice.

3. Election procedure before the Assembly
11. Article 23 of the Convention, paragraphs 1 to 3, at present, stipulates:
“1. The judges shall be elected for a period of nine years. They may not be re-elected.
2. The terms of office of judges shall expire when they reach the age of 70.
3. The judges shall hold office until replaced. They shall, however, continue to deal with such cases as they
already have under consideration.”
12. After the entry into force, on 1 August 2021, of Protocol No. 15 to the Convention, the above-mentioned
paragraph 2 of Article 23 was deleted and the age limit of 70 no longer applies. At the same time, Article 21
paragraph 2, inserted by Protocol No. 15 to the Convention, reads as follows:
“Candidates shall be less than 65 years of age at the date by which the list of three candidates has
been requested by the Parliamentary Assembly, further to Article 22.”

still under 65 years old at the date by which the Secretary General of the Assembly invited the government
to submit a list of candidates (Article 2 of Protocol No. 15).

verdict.summary:
MEMORANDUM — DRAFT FOR ATTORNEY REVIEW. Not legal advice.

Subject: Term of office of judges of the European Court of Human Rights and eligibility for re-election, in the Convention text presented as amended through Protocol No. 15 — correction of the training slide stating 'renewable six-year terms'.

Jurisdiction / legal order: Council of Europe — European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) system. No other legal order is considered or imported.

=====================================================================
I. SOURCES RELIED ON (cited in full)
=====================================================================

[P1] Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (ETS No. 5), as amended by the provisions of Protocol No. 15 (CETS No. 213) with effect from its entry into force on 1 August 2021 and of Protocol No. 14 (CETS No. 194) with effect from its entry into force on 1 June 2010 — consolidated text published by the European Court of Human Rights / Council of Europe, https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/convention_ENG (text of Article 23 quoted at section II below).

[P2] Protocol No. 15 amending the Convention on the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, CETS No. 213, opened for signature 24 June 2013, entered into force 1 August 2021, Article 2(3) and Article 8 (https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/Protocol_15_ENG).

[P3] Explanatory Report to Protocol No. 15, CETS No. 213, paragraphs 10–15 (in particular paragraph 12) (https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/protocol_15_explanatory_report_eng).

[P4] Protocol No. 14 amending the Convention on the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, CETS No. 194, Article 2 (amending Article 23(1) of the Convention), entered into force 1 June 2010. — Cited for the historical step only; see verification flag V-1.

[C1] Council of Europe, Secretariat of the Parliamentary Assembly, Information Note on the election of judges to the European Court of Human Rights, SG-AS (2024) 01 (quoting Article 23(1)–(2) as amended by Protocol No. 15) (https://www.gov.pl/attachment/4cb96533-8779-418e-84e5-c9f09a1885ae). — Corroborative only; not a primary source.

=====================================================================
II. THE GOVERNING TEXT
=====================================================================

[P1], Article 23 ('Terms of office and dismissal'), paragraphs 1–3, in the consolidated text presented as amended through Protocol No. 15:

  '1. The judges shall be elected for a period of nine years. They may not be re-elected.
   2. The judges shall hold office until replaced. They shall, however, continue to deal with such cases as they already have under consideration.
   3. No judge may be dismissed from office unless the other judges decide by a majority of two-thirds that that judge has ceased to fulfil the required conditions.'

Composition of that text:

(a) Paragraph 1 was last amended by Protocol No. 14 (in force 1 June 2010) [P4] and was NOT amended by Protocol No. 15. Protocol No. 15 Article 2(3) provides: 'Paragraph 2 of Article 23 of the Convention shall be deleted. Paragraphs 3 and 4 of Article 23 of the Convention shall become paragraphs 2 and 3 of Article 23 respectively.' [P2].

(b) The paragraph deleted by Protocol No. 15 was the former age-limit provision: 'The terms of office of judges shall expire when they reach the age of 70.' The Explanatory Report confirms this: 'The age limit applied under Article 23, paragraph 2 of the Convention, as drafted prior to the entry into force of this Protocol, had the effect of preventing certain experienced judges from completing their term of office. It was considered no longer essential to impose an age limit, given the fact that judges' terms of office are no longer renewable.' [P3, para. 12].

(c) Protocol No. 15 inserted a new Article 21(2): 'Candidates shall be less than 65 years of age at the date by which the list of three candidates has been requested by the Parliamentary Assembly, further to Article 22.' [P2, Art. 2(1); P1, Art. 21(2)]. By Article 8(1) of Protocol No. 15 and paragraph 14 of the Explanatory Report, that change applies only to judges elected from lists of candidates submitted after entry into force; judges on lists already submitted (including judges in office and judges-elect on 1 August 2021) remain subject to the pre-existing rule, i.e. expiry of term at age 70 [P3, para. 14].

(d) Article 23(2) as now numbered ('The judges shall hold office until replaced...') is a continuity-of-office rule, not a renewal of the mandate. It permits a judge to continue sitting on cases already under consideration after the term expires and pending replacement; it confers no new term.

=====================================================================
III. ANSWERS
=====================================================================

ASK 2 — Election term.
Nine (9) years. Source: [P1], Article 23(1), first sentence: 'The judges shall be elected for a period of nine years.' Election is by the Parliamentary Assembly under Article 22 [P1]. Corroborated by [C1], which quotes the same sentence and states that 'judges are elected for a fixed term of nine years' and that 'judges are able to serve on the Court until the end of their mandate of 9 years' [C1].

ASK 3 — May a judge be re-elected?
No. Source: [P1], Article 23(1), second sentence: 'They may not be re-elected.' The prohibition is unqualified on the face of the text. Corroborated by [P3, para. 12] ('the fact that judges' terms of office are no longer renewable') and by [C1].

Consequence for the maximum period of judicial service: one nine-year term, subject only to the continuation-in-office rule in Article 23(2) [P1] where a judge whose term has expired continues to deal with cases already under consideration and holds office until replaced. That continuation is not a re-election and does not constitute a second term.

=====================================================================
IV. WHY THE SLIDE IS WRONG — AND WHICH INSTRUMENT CORRECTED IT
=====================================================================

The slide's 'renewable six-year terms' is not a misreading of the current text; it is a statement of a superseded text. The correction is not attributable to Protocol No. 15 (a common misattribution, because Protocol No. 15 is the most recent amendment to Article 23). It is attributable to Protocol No. 14.

Chronology (the pre-2010 step is flagged at V-1):

1. Convention as amended by Protocol No. 11 (in force 1 November 1998) — Article 23(1) provided for election 'for a period of six years' with eligibility for re-election. This is the source of the slide's formulation.
2. Protocol No. 14, CETS No. 194 (in force 1 June 2010) — Article 2 replaced Article 23(1) with the nine-year, non-renewable rule [P4].
3. Protocol No. 15, CETS No. 213 (in force 1 August 2021) — deleted former Article 23(2) (age-70 expiry), renumbered paragraphs 3 and 4 as 2 and 3, and added Article 21(2) (candidates under 65) [P2; P3, paras 11–14]. It did not alter the term of office or the re-election prohibition.

So the slide is approximately 15 years out of date (since 1 June 2010), not 4 years out of date (since 1 August 2021).

=====================================================================
V. WHERE AUTHORITY IS THIN, AND VERIFICATION FLAGS
=====================================================================

V-1 (verification required before publication). The six-year/renewable wording of the Protocol No. 11 era, and the precise article numbering of Protocol No. 11 and Protocol No. 14 Article 2, were not re-fetched in this iteration. The Protocol No. 14 entry-into-force date of 1 June 2010 is confirmed on the face of [P1]. Before the note is published, counsel should confirm against the authentic texts of Protocol No. 11 (CETS No. 155) and Protocol No. 14 (CETS No. 194) the exact pre-2010 wording and the article numbers cited at section IV. Neither answer at section III depends on this: both rest on the current consolidated text [P1].

V-2 (thin authority). The scope of 'They may not be re-elected' is unqualified in the text and bars a further term. Whether it would also bar election for a non-consecutive term after an intervening period is not addressed by any judgment of the Court or by any Committee of Ministers instrument identified in this research; the settled practice is a single nine-year term. The point should not be asserted further than the text supports. It is not material to the slide correction.

V-3 (transitional application). Protocol No. 15 contains no transitional provision for Article 23(1) because Protocol No. 15 did not amend it [P2, Art. 8(4)]. Any question about judges elected before 1 June 2010 whose six-year terms were running at the date of the Protocol No. 14 amendment is a historical question; it does not affect the position under the text as amended through Protocol No. 15. Do not state a transitional rule for Protocol No. 14 Article 2 without checking the authentic text (see V-1).

V-4 (source hierarchy). [C1] is a Council of Europe secretariat document, not primary law. It is cited only as corroboration; the operative citations are [P1] and [P2].

=====================================================================
VI. DRAFT REPLACEMENT SLIDE TEXT (for insertion, subject to review)
=====================================================================

Heading: 'Judges of the European Court of Human Rights — tenure'

- Election term: nine years (ECHR, Article 23(1), first sentence, as amended by Protocol No. 14, in force 1 June 2010).
- Re-election: not permitted — 'They may not be re-elected' (ECHR, Article 23(1), second sentence).
- Election body: Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe, from a list of three candidates nominated by the State (ECHR, Article 22).
- Candidate age criterion: candidates must be under 65 at the date the list of three is requested (ECHR, Article 21(2), inserted by Protocol No. 15, in force 1 August 2021; applies only to lists submitted after that date — Protocol No. 15, Article 8(1)).
- Continuation in office: a judge whose term has expired holds office until replaced and continues to deal with cases already under consideration (ECHR, Article 23(2)); this is not a second term.
- Superseded: 'renewable six-year terms' was the position under the Convention as amended by Protocol No. 11 (1998–2010) and has not been correct since 1 June 2010.

=====================================================================
VII. CAVEAT
=====================================================================

This memorandum is a draft prepared for review by a qualified attorney. It is not legal advice and should not be relied on as such. Every statement of law above is tied to the primary source cited at the point at which it is made; where authority is thin or unverified, that is stated at section V rather than resolved.

quotes.whole: The following cost categories exclusively, and only if they result from the closure of coal production units: (a) the cost of paying social welfare benefits resulting from the pensioning-off of workers before they reach statutory retirement age; (b) other exceptional expenditure on workers who have lost or who lose their jobs; (c) the payment of pensions and allowances outside the statutory system to workers who have lost or who lose their jobs and to workers entitled to such payments before the closure; (d) the cost covered by the undertakings for the readaptation of workers in order to help them find new jobs outside the coal industry, especially training costs; (e) the supply of free coal to workers who have lost or who lose their jobs and to workers entitled to such supply before the closure, or the monetary equivalent; (f) residual costs resulting from administrative, legal or tax provisions which are specific to the coal industry; (g) additional underground safety work resulting from the closure of coal production units; (h) mining damage, provided that it has been caused by the coal production units which have been closed or which are being closed; (i) all duly justified costs related to the rehabilitation of former coal mining sites, including: — residual costs resulting from contributions to bodies responsible for water supplies and for the removal of waste water, — other residual costs resulting from water supplies and the removal of waste water; (j) residual costs to cover former miners’ health insurance; (k) costs related to the cancelling or modification of ongoing contracts (for a maximum value of 6 months of production); (l) exceptional intrinsic depreciation provided that it results from the closure of coal production units; (m) costs of surface recultivation.

quotes.whole: Article 1U.K.Definitions For the purposes of this Decision, the following definitions shall apply: (a) ‘coal’ means high-grade, medium-grade and low-grade category A and B coal within the meaning of the international codification system for coal laid down by the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe(1); (b) ‘closure’ means the permanent cessation of production and sale of coal; (c) ‘closure plan’ means a plan drawn up by a Member State providing for measures culminating in the definitive closure of coal production units; (d) ‘coal production unit’ means underground or opencast coal workings and related infrastructure capable of producing raw coal independently of other parts of the undertaking; (e) ‘coal year’ means calendar year or another 12-month period used as a reference for contracts in the coal industry; (f) ‘production costs’ means total costs related to current production, including mining operations, operations for the dressing of coal, in particular washing, sizing and sorting, and transport to the utilization point, normal depreciation and market-based interest charges on borrowed capital; (g) ‘current production losses’ means the positive difference between the coal production cost and the selling price at utilisation point freely agreed between the contracting parties in the light of the conditions prevailing on the world market.

verdict.summary:
# MEMORANDUM — DRAFT FOR ATTORNEY REVIEW — NOT LEGAL ADVICE

**To:** State-aid team (instructing client)
**From:** Legal researcher
**Re:** Whether Commission Regulation (EU) No 651/2014 can be relied on to exempt aid to facilitate the closure of an uncompetitive coal mine from notification; and, if not, the instrument the Regulation's scope passage identifies
**Jurisdiction:** European Union — State aid under Articles 107 and 108 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU), Council Decision 2010/787/EU, and Commission Regulation (EU) No 651/2014
**Status:** Research draft. Not legal advice; not for filing with the Commission as it stands.

---

## I. Questions presented

1. Can a State-aid team rely on Commission Regulation (EU) No 651/2014 (the General Block Exemption Regulation, 'GBER') to exempt from the notification requirement of Article 108(3) TFEU aid to facilitate the closure of an uncompetitive coal mine?
2. If not, which instrument does the Regulation's scope passage identify as dealing with that aid?

## II. Short answers

1. **No.** Aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines is excluded from the GBER's scope outright by Article 1(2)(d) of Regulation 651/2014, and rectical 12 says the Regulation 'should not apply' to it. The block exemption operates only for aid that satisfies 'the conditions laid down in this Article and in Chapter I'; Article 1 is the Chapter I gate. This is a scope exclusion, not a discretionary refusal, so there is no route to exemption by arging compatibility.
2. **Council Decision 2010/787/EU of 10 December 2010 on State aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines (OJ L 336, 21.12.2010, p. 24).** Both the scope passage (Article 1(2)(d)) and rectical 12 name it.

---

## III. Primary sources relied on (cited in full)

| # | Source | Citation | Provisions used |
|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | Commission Regulation (EU) No 651/2014 of 17 June 2014 declaring certain categories of aid compatible with the internal market in application of Article 107 and 108 of the Treaty | OJ L 187, 26.6.2014, p. 1 | Art. 1(1), 1(2) intro and (d), 1(2) second subpara., 1(4); Art. 2(13); recital 12; the Chapter I conditioning formula in Arts. 33–35 |
| S2 | Commission Regulation (EU) 2017/1084 of 14 June 2017 amending Regulation (EU) No 651/2014 as regards aid for port and airport infrastructure, notification thresholds for aid for culture and heritage conservation and for aid for sport and multifunctional recreational infrastructures, and regional operating aid schemes for outermost regions, and amending Regulation (EU) No 702/2014 as regards the calculation of eligible costs | OJ (2017) — as consolidated on legislation.gov.uk, footnote F1 to Art. 1 | Amends Art. 1(2)(d) and its footnote (2) |
| S3 | Council Decision 2010/787/EU of 10 December 2010 on State aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines | OJ L 336, 21.12.2010, p. 24 | Arts. 1, 2, 3, 4 and Annex; Arts. 6, 7, 8; Art. 9 (entry into force, application, expiry) |
| S4 | Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union | Consolidated version | Arts. 107(3), 108(3) (as cross-referenced in S1) |

Text consulted as fetched: EUR-Lex text of S1 (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=uriserv:OJ.L_.2014.187.01.0001.01.ENG); EUR-Lex text of S3 (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dec/2010/787/oj); legislation.gov.uk adopted texts of S1 Art. 1 and body, and the 2017-07-10 revised version of S1 Art. 1; legislation.gov.uk text of S3.

---

## IV. Why the GBER does not exempt this aid

### A. The GBER is an exhaustive, closed list plus a closed list of exclusions

Article 1(1) of S1 provides that the Regulation 'shall apply to the following categories of aid' and then lists them: (a) regional aid; (b) aid to SMEs; (c) aid for environmental protection; (d) R&D&I; (e) training aid; (f) recruitment and employment aid for disadvantaged workers and workers with disabilities; (g) natural-disaster aid; (h) social aid for transport for residents of remote regions; (i) broadband; (j) culture and heritage; (k) sport and multifunctional recreational infrastructure; (l) local infrastructure. Coal-mine closure aid appears nowhere on that list.

Article 1(2) then provides: 'This Regulation shall not apply to:' and includes at point (d) 'aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines, as covered by Council Decision No 2010/787' (as adopted in 2014; since S2 the reference reads 'Council Decision 2010/787/EU'). The exclusion is doubly secured: the category is not within Article 1(1), and it is expressly excluded by Article 1(2)(d).

### B. The block exemption is conditioned on Chapter I, of which Article 1 is the first provision

The operative exempting articles in S1 use a uniform formula. By way of illustration, Article 33 provides that aid 'shall be compatible with the internal market within the meaning of Article 107(3) of the Treaty and shall be exempt from the notification requirement of Article 108(3) of the Treaty, provided the conditions laid down in this Article and in Chapter I are fulfilled.' Articles 34 and 35 are worded identically. Article 1 sits in Chapter I. Aid excluded by Article 1(2) therefore can never satisfy 'the conditions laid down ... in Chapter I', and no amount of compliance with an operative article (for example the training or environmental aid articles) cures the defect.

### C. Recital 12 confirms the intent and, importantly, does not leave coal in a gap

Recital 12 of S1: 'This Regulation should not apply to aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines, which is dealt with by the Council Decision of 10 December 2010 on State aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines. This Regulation should apply to other types of aid in the coal sector, with the exception of regional aid.'

Two consequences follow. First, the exclusion is deliberate and tied to a named alternative instrument, so it is not a drafting omission that could be read down. Second, the GBER is **not** closed to the coal sector as a whole: non-closure aid in the coal sector can still be block-exempted under the relevant Chapter III heading, save for regional aid (rectical 12, final sentence, read with Article 1(2)(e)). The dividing line is therefore functional — is the aid 'to facilitate the closure of an uncompetitive coal mine'? — not sectoral.

### D. The definition of 'coal' in the GBER is parasitic on the Decision

Article 2(13) of S1: "'coal' means high-grade, medium-grade and low-grade category A and B coal within the meaning of the international codification system for coal established by the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe and clarified in the Council decision of 10 December 2010 on State aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines.' The GBER does not run its own coal test; it borrows the Decision's (S3, Article 1(a), worded in materially identical terms). This confirms the two instruments are designed as a single scheme.

### E. The separation-of-activities carve-out does not reach point (d)

The second subparagraph of Article 1(2) of S1 allows an undertak active in excluded sectors to receive GBER aid for its in-scope activities, subject to separation of activities or distinction of costs. But by its own words it applies only 'where an undertak is active in the excluded sectors as referred to in points (a), (b) or (c) of the first subparagraph'. Point (d) — coal-mine closure aid — is not listed. The carve-out therefore cannot be used to bring closure aid back in, and it cannot be used to fund the mine's closure costs through the mine's other activities.

### F. Two independent bars that will often apply on the facts of an uncompetitive mine

Even if a measure escaped Article 1(2)(d), Article 1(4) of S1 provides that the Regulation 'shall not apply to: (a) aid schemes which do not explicitly exclude the payment of individual aid in favour of an undertak which is subject to an outstanding recovery order following a previous Commission decision declaring an aid illegal and incompatible with the internal market ...; (b) ad hoc aid in favour of an undertak as referred to in point (a); (c) aid to undertak in difficulty, with the exception of aid schemes to make good the damage caused by certain natural disasters.' An uncompetitive mine operator is frequently an undertak in difficulty and sometimes carries legacy recovery exposure. Either fact pattern is a second, independent scope bar, and rectical on the point confirms the policy ('Aid granted to undertak in difficulty should be excluded from the scope of this Regulation ... in order to avoid their circumvention').

### G. What the GBER does still reach in this area

Subject to the functional line in C above, the following GBER headings are not excluded merely because the beneficiary is a coal undertak: training aid (Art. 31), recruitment and employment aid for disadvantaged workers and workers with disabilities (Arts. 32–35), environmental investment aid going beyond Union standards (Art. 36 ff.), and, where the conditions fit, energy-efficient district heating and cooling (Art. 46) and energy infrastructure (Art. 48). Whether a given measure is 'aid to facilitate closure' (and so excluded) or genuinely separate aid is the hard question — see section VII.

---

## V. The instrument the scope passage identifies: Decision 2010/787/EU

### A. Status and architecture

S3 is a Council Decision of 10 December 2010. By Article 9 it enters into force on the day following publication, 'shall apply from 1 January 2011', and 'shall expire on 31 December 2027'. Its own recticals describe it as marking 'the transition, for the coal sector, from the application of sector-specific rules to the application of general State aid rules which are applicable to all sectors.'

Article 1 defines: (a) 'coal' — high-grade, medium-grade and low-grade category A and B coal per the UNECE codification; (b) 'closure' — 'the permanent cessation of production and sale of coal'; (c) 'closure plan'; (d) 'coal production unit'; (e) 'coal year'; (f) 'production costs'; (g) 'current production losses'. Article 2(1) states the principle: 'In the context of closure of uncompetitive mines, aid to the coal industry may be considered compatible with the proper functioning of the internal market if it complies with the provisions of this Decision.' Article 2(2) limits aid to coal used for electricity, combined heat and power, coke, and blast-furnace fuelling in the steel industry, where that use takes place in the Union.

### B. Article 3 — closure aid, and the 31 December 2018 gate

Article 3(1) makes aid 'intended specifically to cover the current production losses of coal production units' compatible only if, among other conditions: (a) 'the operation of the coal production units concerned must form part of a closure plan the deadline of which does not extend beyond 31 December 2018'; (b) the units 'must be closed definitively in accordance with the closure plan'; and (c) the aid notified must not exceed the difference between foreseeable production costs and foreseeable revenue for a coal year, with annual correction. Article 3(3) provides that if the units are not closed at the date fixed in the authorised closure plan, 'the Member State concerned shall recover all aid granted in respect of the whole period covered by the closure plan.' The Decision also requires a Member State intending to grant Article 3 closure aid to notify a closure plan for the units concerned to the Commission (paragraph number to be confirmed against the OJ text — the sentence appears in the Article 3 context in the text consulted).

### C. Article 4 — aid to cover exceptional costs

Article 4(1) covers State aid to undertaks which carry out or have carried out a coal-production activity, to enable them to cover costs 'arising from or having arisen from the closure of coal production units and which are not related to current production', up to the amount of such costs, whether incurred by one undertak or several. Article 4(2) refers to the Annex for the closed list of cost categories and states that paragraph 1 'shall not apply to costs resulting from non-compliance with environmental regulations.' The Annex list includes, among others: social welfare benefits from early pensioning-off; other exceptional expenditure on workers who have lost or lose their jobs; pensions and allowances outside the statutory system; readaptation and training costs; free coal or its monetary equivalent; residual costs from coal-specific administrative, legal or tax provisions; additional underground safety work; mining damage caused by the units being closed; duly justified rehabilitation costs of former coal-mining sites; residual costs of former miners' health insurance; cancelling or modification of ongoing contracts (capped at six months of production); exceptional intrinsic depreciation resulting from closure; and surface recultivation.

### D. Supervision provisions

Article 6 (separation of accounts), Article 7 (information to be provided by Member States), Article 8 (implementing measures) complete the scheme. These are the machinery that replaces the GBER's own Chapter I conditions; they are why the Commission can say the aid 'is dealt with by' the Decision.

---

## VI. Decision tree by date of grant (the temporal point counsel must fix before relying on anything)

| Date aid is to be granted | Route | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| On or before 31 Dec 2018, with a closure plan deadline no later than 31 Dec 2018 | Article 3 closure aid possible; notify closure plan to the Commission | S3 Arts. 3(1)(a), 3(3) |
| 1 Jan 2019 – 31 Dec 2027 | Article 3 closure aid for current production losses practically unavailable (the 2018 plan deadline cannot be met); Article 4 aid for Annex exceptional costs remains textually open until the Decision expires | S3 Arts. 3(1)(a), 4, 9 |
| After 31 Dec 2027 | No block exemption (S1 Art. 1(2)(d)) and no sectoral framework (S3 Art. 9 expiry). Notification under Art. 108(3) TFEU and direct assessment under Art. 107(3) TFEU | S1 Art. 1(2)(d); S3 Art. 9; S4 |

In every branch the GBER is unavailable for the closure aid itself. The only variable is which notification route replaces it.

---

## VII. Where authority is thin, conflicting or unverified — read before advising

1. **Hard coal versus lignite.** S3 Art. 1(a) and S1 Art. 2(13) define 'coal' by reference to the UNECE codification, categories A and B. The working reading is that this covers hard coal and excludes brown coal/lignite, which would put a lignite mine outside both instruments — no block exemption and no sectoral framework, hence direct Article 107(3)/108(3). **The UNECE codification itself was not retrieved for this draft.** Confirm before advising on any non-hard-coal site.
2. **Article 4 after 2018.** The 31 Dec 2018 deadline sits in Article 3(1)(a), not in Article 4. Textually, Article 4 aid for residual and exceptional closure costs is not subject to it. Whether the Commission would accept Article 4 aid for a mine that only closes after 2018 is not resolved by the text; pre-notification contact is advisable.
3. **Overlap between Decision Annex items and GBER headings.** Readaptation/training, social welfare benefits and site rehabilitation appear both in the S3 Annex and, in generalized form, under GBER training and environmental aid. Whether a given measure is 'aid to facilitate the closure' (S1 Art. 1(2)(d), excluded) or a genuinely separate in-scope measure is not settled by either text. The risk is that a package split across GBER headings is treated as a single measure; no case law was retrieved for this draft on that point and none is asserted here.
4. **Article 4(2) environmental carve-out.** Rehabilitation costs that remedy non-compliance with environmental regulations are expressly outside Article 4. This is an easy trap in a closure budget and should be screened line by line against the Annex.
5. **GBER period of application.** Article 58 of S1 fixes the Regulation's period of application and that period has been prolonged by amending regulations. The relevant text was not retrieved; the memo therefore makes no assertion about a GBER end date. Confirm the consolidated version in force at the intended grant date, and confirm that Article 1(2)(d) has not been further amended after S2.
6. **Legal basis of S3.** The Decision's preamble (which would show its Treaty basis) was not captured in the passages consulted. Not material to the two answers, but should be cited correctly in any notification.
7. **Citation form.** The 2014 adopted text of Art. 1(2)(d) reads 'Council Decision No 2010/787'; S2 corrected the reference and added the full OJ footnote. Quote the version in force at the relevant date.

---

## VIII. Practical consequence of getting this wrong

Aid that is neither block-exempted nor notified is granted in breach of the standstill obligation in Article 108(3) TFEU (the very obligation the GBER articles dispense with — see the formula in S1 Arts. 33–35). The exposure is a Commission decision declaring the aid illegal and incompatible, with recovery from the beneficiary, plus the Article 3(3) recovery mechanism under the Decision if a closure plan is not honoured. The correct default where scope is doubtful is notification, not reliance on the block exemption.

---

## IX. Verification checklist for counsel

- [ ] Confirm the Member State and the intended grant date; select the branch in section VI.
- [ ] Confirm the coal type against the UNECE codification (item 1).
- [ ] Confirm the consolidated version of S1 in force at the grant date, including whether Art. 1(2)(d) has changed since S2.
- [ ] Screen the closure budget against the S3 Annex, excluding environmental non-compliance costs (item 4).
- [ ] Confirm the paragraph numbering of the closure-plan notification sentence in Art. 3.
- [ ] If any part of the package is proposed under a GBER heading, document the separation of activities and costs and test the 'aid to facilitate closure' boundary (item 3).

---

## X. One-line answers for the file

1. **No** — Regulation (EU) No 651/2014 cannot be relied on; Art. 1(2)(d) excludes the aid from scope, and rectical 12 says the Regulation 'should not apply'.
2. **Council Decision 2010/787/EU of 10 December 2010 on State aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines (OJ L 336, 21.12.2010, p. 24)** — named by both Art. 1(2)(d) and rectical 12.

quotes.whole: The considerations giving rise to the application of Article 15 gradually become less forceful and relevant as the public emergency threatening the life of the nation, while still persisting, declines in intensity. The exigency criterion must therefore be applied more stringently (Baş v. Turkey, 2020, § 224). The Court does accept that when a State is struggling against a public emergency threatening the life of the nation, it would be rendered defenceless if it were required to accomplish everything at once, to furnish from the outset each of its chosen means of action with each of the safeguards reconcilable with the priority requirements for the proper functioning of the authorities and for restoring peace within the community. The interpretation of Article 15 of the Convention must leave a place for progressive adaptations (ibid., § 229). Nevertheless, in the case of an interference with a fundamental Convention right, given the potentially adverse impact it entails, the Court will examine whether the interference is still strictly required for the preservation of public safety (ibid., § 230).

February 2022
This Factsheet does not bind the Court and is not exhaustive
Derogation in time of emergency
Article 15 (derogation in time of emergency) of the European Convention on
Human Rights1 affords to the governments of the States parties, in exceptional
circumstances, the possibility of derogating, in a temporary, limited and supervised
manner, from their obligation to secure certain rights and freedoms under the
